topics.name: Airport ops & radio
facts: Nontowered airport: monitor CTAF and make your first call about 10 NM out, then downwind, base, final, and clear of the runway.
Pilot-controlled lighting: 7 clicks in 5 seconds = high, 5 = medium, 3 = low. Start with 7.

Sign colors: red with white text = mandatory (hold here). Black with yellow text = location (where you are). Yellow with black text = direction or destination. Outbound destination signs point to takeoff runways.
Runway numbers are the magnetic heading divided by 10: Runway 9 = 090° magnetic, Runway 27 = 270° magnetic.
Runway/runway hold position sign (red, e.g. 15-33) marks an intersecting runway.
VASI guarantees obstruction clearance within ±10° of centerline out to 4 NM. In Class D airspace, stay at or above the glide slope (91.129). Red over white = on glidepath.
Segmented circle: pick the runway most aligned with the wind. The short leg of the L shows which way the pattern turns.
Emergency and not talking to ATC: squawk 7700 and call on 121.5 MHz.

Airport beacon: white-green = civil land airport, white-yellow = water, two white flashes then green = military. A daytime beacon in Class B–E surface areas often means the weather is below VFR minimums.
Lights: runway edge white (yellow on the last 2,000 ft of instrument runways), threshold green toward you, runway end red. Taxiway edge blue, centerline green.
Displaced threshold (arrows): taxi, take off and roll out, but don't touch down before it. Chevrons: don't use at all. A yellow or white X: closed.
Transponder: 1200 VFR, 7500 hijack, 7600 lost communications, 7700 emergency. 121.5 MHz is the emergency frequency.
Scan in 10° sectors, about 1 second each. An aircraft with no relative motion is on a collision course.

topics.name: Airspace & regulations
facts: ELT battery: replace or recharge after 1 cumulative hour of use or when 50% of its useful life has expired (91.207). The ELT itself is inspected every 12 calendar months.
National parks, monuments and wildlife refuges: stay at least 2,000 ft above the surface.
Class A (18,000 ft MSL to FL600) is IFR only. VFR flight is prohibited.
ADS-B Out is required in Class A, B and C airspace, inside the 30 NM Mode C veil, and at or above 10,000 ft MSL (except at or below 2,500 ft AGL).
Preflight action (91.103), NWKRAFT: NOTAMs, Weather, Known ATC delays, Runway lengths, Alternatives, Fuel, Takeoff and landing distances.
Alert area: every pilot inside is responsible for collision avoidance.
Medical: third class lasts 60 months if you were under 40 at the exam, 24 months at 40 or older. Flight review: every 24 calendar months (1 h ground + 1 h flight).
Passengers: 3 takeoffs and landings in the last 90 days; at night (1 h after sunset to 1 h before sunrise) they must be full-stop.
Alcohol: 8 hours bottle to throttle and under 0.04 BAC. Fuel reserve: 30 minutes day, 45 minutes night.
Right-of-way: aircraft in distress first; converging, the one on the right; head-on, both turn right; overtaking, pass on the right; balloon > glider > airship > airplane.
Inspections: annual every 12 calendar months, 100-hour if used for hire, transponder every 24 months, ELT every 12 months (battery after 1 h of use or 50% of its life).
Oxygen: crew above 12,500 ft after 30 minutes, crew at all times above 14,000 ft, every occupant provided oxygen above 15,000 ft.
Paperwork on board: ARROW. Day VFR equipment: ATOMATOFLAMES; night adds FLAPS.
VFR cruising more than 3,000 ft AGL: magnetic course 0–179° odd thousands + 500, 180–359° even thousands + 500.

topics.name: Aerodynamics
facts: A wing always stalls at the same critical angle of attack. Weight, bank and load factor change the stall SPEED, not the stall angle.
Load factor in a level turn = 1 ÷ cos(bank). 30° ≈ 1.15 G, 45° ≈ 1.41 G, 60° = 2 G. Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor (+41% at 60°).
Ground effect works within about one wingspan of the surface. Less downwash and wingtip vortex means less induced drag, so you float if you're fast in the flare.
Leaving ground effect brings induced drag back. If you're below climb speed, the airplane can settle back onto the runway.
A heavier airplane stalls at a higher speed, needs longer takeoff and landing rolls, and climbs more slowly.
A spin needs a stall: both wings stalled, one more than the other.
Load factor = 1 ÷ cos(bank): 1.41 G at 45°, 2 G at 60°. Stall speed rises with √G (about +41% at 60°).
Maneuvering speed (Va) decreases as weight decreases. Normal category limits: +3.8 G and −1.52 G.
Forward CG: more stable, higher stall speed, harder to flare. Aft CG: less stable, harder stall and spin recovery.
Left-turning tendencies: torque, P-factor, spiraling slipstream and gyroscopic precession.
Airspeed arcs: white Vs0–Vfe, green Vs1–Vno, yellow Vno–Vne (smooth air only), red line Vne. Va isn't marked.

topics.name: Wake turbulence & collision avoidance
facts: Wake turbulence = wingtip vortices. They exist only while a wing makes lift, from rotation to nosewheel touchdown.
Vortices sink 300 to 500 fpm and level off 500 to 1,000 ft below the flight path. A light quartering tailwind is the worst case.
Landing behind a large aircraft: stay at or above its path and touch down beyond its touchdown point. Taking off behind one: lift off before its rotation point.
Strongest vortices: heavy, clean (gear and flaps up) and slow.
Daytime scan: short steps of about 10°, pausing about 1 second on each. Night: scan slowly and use off-center viewing.
Vortices start at rotation and end at touchdown. They are strongest when the airplane is heavy, clean and slow.
They sink 300–500 fpm, level off 500–1,000 ft below the flight path and drift 2–3 kt near the ground. A light quartering tailwind is the worst case.
Land beyond a jet's touchdown point. Take off before its rotation point (or past its touchdown point if it just landed).

topics.name: Performance & weight and balance
facts: Vy = most altitude in the least time. Vx = most altitude in the least distance (obstacles).
Moment = weight × arm. CG = total moment ÷ total weight. Avgas weighs 6 lb/gal.
To move the CG aft, add weight aft or move it aft. To move it forward, do the reverse.
High, hot and humid = high density altitude = longer takeoff roll and weaker climb.
Pressure altitude = elevation + (29.92 − altimeter setting) × 1,000. Density altitude ≈ pressure altitude + 120 ft per °C above standard (15°C at sea level, −2°C per 1,000 ft).
Hot, high and humid means high density altitude: longer takeoff and a weaker climb.
A 10% headwind cuts takeoff distance about 19%; a 10% tailwind adds about 21%; 10% more weight adds at least 21%.
Moment = weight × arm; CG = total moment ÷ total weight. Shifting weight: weight moved ÷ total weight = CG change ÷ distance moved.
Avgas 6 lb/gal, oil 7.5 lb/gal. Crosswind ≈ wind × sin(angle): 30° → 50%, 45° → 70%, 60° → 90%.

topics.name: Instruments & systems
facts: No altimeter setting available: set the altimeter to the departure airport's elevation (91.121).
Attitude indicator: the knob moves the miniature airplane. In level flight, align it with the horizon bar.

Pilot-adjustable: altimeter (Kollsman window), heading indicator (realign with the compass about every 15 min), and the attitude indicator's miniature airplane. The airspeed indicator and VSI have no pilot adjustment.
Static port blocked: altimeter freezes, VSI reads zero, airspeed is wrong. Pitot blocked: only the airspeed indicator is affected.
GPS altitude is geometric. It's a cross-check only, so fly the barometric altimeter.
Airspeed indicator uses pitot and static; altimeter and VSI use static only. Pitot and drain blocked: the ASI acts like an altimeter. Static blocked: the altimeter freezes.
High to low (pressure or temperature), look out below: your true altitude is lower than indicated.
Compass errors: UNOS (undershoot north, overshoot south in turns), ANDS (accelerate north, decelerate south on east-west headings).
Carb ice: 20–70°F with high humidity; first sign is an RPM drop with a fixed-pitch prop. Carb heat makes the mixture richer.
Detonation: lower the nose, enrich the mixture, reduce power. Never use a lower grade of fuel than specified. 100LL is blue.

topics.name: Weather
facts: METAR and TAF winds are TRUE. ATIS and tower winds are MAGNETIC.
Wind code dddssGggKT: 11012G18KT = from 110° true at 12 kt, gusting to 18 kt.
Significant Weather Prog charts are forecasts. Use them to find areas to avoid (turbulence, freezing levels, IFR).
Ceiling = the lowest BKN or OVC layer (or VV). Heights are in hundreds of feet AGL.
Standard lapse rate: 2°C per 1,000 ft. Cumulus base ≈ temperature/dew point spread ÷ 2.5°C (or ÷ 4.4°F) × 1,000 ft.
Stable air: stratiform clouds, smooth air, poor visibility, steady rain. Unstable air: cumuliform clouds, turbulence, good visibility, showers.
Thunderstorms need moisture, instability and lift. Stages: cumulus (updrafts), mature (rain at the surface), dissipating (downdrafts). Avoid severe ones by 20 NM.
Fog: radiation (clear calm nights), advection (moist air moving over a cold surface, needs wind), upslope, steam.
AIRMET Sierra (IFR, mountain obscuration), Tango (turbulence, surface winds ≥ 30 kt), Zulu (icing). SIGMET: severe icing or turbulence, dust or sand, volcanic ash.
Winds aloft (FB): true direction, knots and °C. A direction code above 36 means subtract 50 from the direction and add 100 kt. 9900 is light and variable.

topics.name: Navigation & charts
facts: Magenta vignette: Class E starts at 700 ft AGL. Blue vignette: 1,200 ft AGL. Dashed magenta: Class E to the surface.
A bracketed number like [29] is the Class D ceiling in hundreds of feet MSL (2,900 ft).
Magenta flags = VFR checkpoints. A frequency followed by ⓒ = CTAF. 'CT – 126.0 ★' = tower frequency, part-time.
Stay on course with a wind-corrected heading and checkpoints every 10 to 20 NM. If you're lost: Climb, Communicate, Confess, Comply, Conserve.
1° of latitude = 60 NM. Measure true course at the meridian near the middle of the route.
True course ± wind correction = true heading; ± variation (east is least, west is best) = magnetic heading; ± deviation = compass heading.
VOR radials are magnetic, FROM the station. Full-scale CDI = 10°. VOT and ground checks ±4°, airborne ±6°. A VOT centers at 360 FROM or 180 TO.
Sectional colors: Class B solid blue, C solid magenta, D dashed blue, E surface dashed magenta, E from 700 ft AGL magenta vignette.
Lost: climb, communicate, confess, comply (and conserve fuel). An open VFR flight plan triggers a search 30 minutes after your ETA.

topics.name: Maneuvers, emergencies & ADM
facts: Hazardous attitudes and their antidotes: Antiauthority (follow the rules), Impulsivity (not so fast), Invulnerability (it could happen to me), Macho (taking chances is foolish), Resignation (I'm not helpless).
Split flaps: the airplane rolls toward the wing with LESS flap and yaws toward the EXTENDED flap. Use opposite aileron and opposite rudder (cross-controlled), and keep your airspeed up.
Rectangular course: turns onto and off the upwind leg are less than 90° (shallow bank). Turns at the downwind end are more than 90° (steepest bank).
Flaps lower the stall speed and add drag, so slow flight with flaps is slower and needs more power.
Soft-field takeoff: hold the nose high to get weight off the nosewheel, then stay in ground effect to accelerate.
Hypoxia types: hypoxic (altitude), hypemic (carbon monoxide), stagnant (poor circulation), histotoxic (alcohol, drugs).

Hazardous attitudes and antidotes: anti-authority / follow the rules; impulsivity / not so fast; invulnerability / it could happen to me; macho / taking chances is foolish; resignation / I'm not helpless.
IMSAFE checks the pilot, PAVE groups the risks, DECIDE and 3P (perceive, process, perform) guide decisions.
Landing illusions: a narrow or upsloping runway, rain or a black-hole approach make you fly too low; a wide or downsloping runway makes you fly too high.
Night: 30 minutes to dark-adapt; look slightly off-center. Only a red light = aircraft crossing right to left; white = moving away; red and green = head-on.
Engine failure: best glide, best field, checklist. Right after takeoff, land roughly straight ahead. Electrical fire: master switch off.

cards.q: When approaching a nontowered airport, when should you make your first position call?
cards.why: AIM 4-1-9: monitor CTAF and self-announce about 10 miles out, then on entering downwind, base, final, and when leaving the runway.

cards.q: What effect does high density altitude have on aircraft performance?
c: It reduces performance: longer takeoff roll, lower climb rate, less engine power
It has no effect on takeoff distance
cards.why: Thin air hurts the wing, the propeller, and the engine at the same time. High, hot, and humid all raise density altitude.

cards.q: When must the battery in an emergency locator transmitter (ELT) be replaced (or recharged if rechargeable)?
c: After one-half (50%) of the battery's useful life, or after 1 cumulative hour of use
cards.why: 14 CFR 91.207. Remember '1 hour or 50%.' Don't confuse it with the 12-month ELT inspection.

cards.q: If an altimeter setting is not available before flight, to which altitude should the pilot adjust the altimeter?
c: The elevation of the departure airport
The elevation of the nearest airport corrected to mean sea level
Pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature
cards.why: 14 CFR 91.121. With no setting available, dial the altimeter until it reads the field elevation where you're sitting.

cards.orig: (Refer to figure 25, area 2.) The control tower frequency for Addison Airport is…
cards.q: Where on a sectional chart do you find an airport's control tower frequency?
c: In the airport data block after 'CT –' (a star ★ means part-time)
In the box under the nearest VOR's name
cards.why: Example: 'CT – 126.0 ★'. When a part-time tower closes, its frequency usually becomes the CTAF (shown as ⓒ).

cards.q: The numbers 9 and 27 on a runway indicate that the runway is oriented approximately
cards.why: Runway numbers are magnetic headings rounded to the nearest 10°, with the last zero dropped.

cards.q: (Figure 12) What are the wind conditions at Wink, Texas (KINK)?
c: 110° true at 12 knots, gusting to 18 knots
110° magnetic at 12 knots, gusting to 18 knots
cards.why: The KINK METAR reports 11012G18KT. That's 3 digits for direction, 2 for speed, and G for gusts. Winds in METARs and TAFs are TRUE, so the 'magnetic' choice is the trap.

cards.q: The best method to use when looking for other traffic at night is to
c: look to the side of the object and scan slowly
scan the visual field very rapidly
look to the side of the object and scan rapidly
cards.why: The rods that handle night vision sit off-center in the eye. Looking slightly to the side of a light keeps it on the rods.

cards.q: In order for an airplane to spin, at least one wing must be
c: producing more lift than the other wing
cards.why: A spin is an aggravated stall with autorotation. No stall, no spin.

cards.orig: (Refer to Figure 21, area 1.) What is the Common Traffic Advisory Frequency (CTAF)…
cards.q: How is the CTAF shown on a sectional chart?
c: A frequency followed by ⓒ (a white C in a dark circle) in the airport data block
A frequency printed inside a blue box
cards.why: ⓒ marks the CTAF. At a part-time tower, the tower frequency is the CTAF when the tower is closed.

cards.q: (Figure 23) The magenta flag symbols at Statesboro Bullock County, Claxton-Evans County, and Ridgeland airports are
c: visual checkpoints used to identify position for the initial callup before entering Savannah Class C airspace
outer boundaries of the Savannah Class C airspace
cards.why: Flags = VFR checkpoints.

cards.q: In the event of an asymmetric (split) flap condition, what control inputs should you use?
c: Opposite aileron to stop the roll and opposite rudder to stop the yaw (a cross-controlled condition)
Aileron and rudder both in the direction of the roll
No input. Retract the other flap and the airplane will correct itself
cards.why: The wing with more flap makes more lift, so the airplane ROLLS toward the wing with less flap. The extended flap also adds drag, so it YAWS toward the extended flap. Counter both and keep your airspeed up. Cross-controlled flight near a stall is dangerous.

cards.q: What does the outbound destination sign identify?
c: Directions to the ramp, terminal, or FBO
The taxiway you are currently on
cards.why: Destination signs are yellow with black text and an arrow. Outbound signs point to takeoff runways; inbound signs point to the ramp or FBO. A black sign with yellow text is a location sign: where you ARE.

cards.q: Unless otherwise authorized, which situation requires Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) Out?
c: Operating within 30 NM of a Class B primary airport (the Mode C veil)
Operating in Class G airspace below 1,200 ft AGL
cards.why: ADS-B Out is required in Class A, B and C airspace, inside the Mode C veil, and at or above 10,000 ft MSL (except at or below 2,500 AGL). Class D doesn't require it.

cards.q: If the pitot tube and outside static vents become clogged, which instruments would be affected?
c: Altimeter, airspeed indicator, and vertical speed indicator
Altimeter, attitude indicator, and turn coordinator
Airspeed indicator, heading indicator, and altimeter
cards.why: These are the three pitot-static instruments. For a static blockage, use the alternate static source.

cards.q: After takeoff, which airspeed would the pilot use to gain the most altitude in a given period of time?
cards.why: Vy is about TIME (feet per minute). Vx is about DISTANCE (feet per mile, for clearing obstacles). Memory aid: 'X' has angles.

cards.q: Responsibility for collision avoidance in an alert area rests with
cards.why: Alert areas have heavy training or unusual activity. All pilots inside, participating or just passing through, are responsible.

cards.q: Pilots flying over a national wildlife refuge are requested to fly no lower than
cards.why: The same 2,000 ft request applies over national parks, monuments, seashores and wilderness areas.

cards.q: How can a pilot use GPS altitude in flight?
c: As a situational-awareness cross-check only. Fly altitudes and terrain clearance using the barometric altimeter
In place of the altimeter whenever no altimeter setting is available
cards.why: GPS altitude is geometric and can differ from barometric altitude by hundreds of feet. ATC and other traffic all use barometric altitude.

cards.q: When are non-rechargeable batteries of an emergency locator transmitter (ELT) required to be replaced?
c: When 50% of their useful life has expired, or after 1 cumulative hour of use
cards.why: Same rule as the ELT battery question (91.207). '12 months' is the ELT inspection interval, not the battery rule.

cards.q: What will happen during takeoff if you attempt to leave ground effect without sufficient airspeed?
c: Induced drag rises as you climb out of ground effect, so the airplane may not climb and can settle back onto the runway
Induced drag decreases and the airplane accelerates
The airplane will climb normally once it is out of ground effect
cards.why: Ground effect lets an airplane lift off below its normal climb speed. Once it's out of ground effect, induced drag comes back and more thrust is needed. Below the recommended speed, it can sink back or stall.

cards.q: The list of required items for a preflight visual inspection should come from:
c: The manufacturer's POH/AFM for that airplane
A generic checklist for the aircraft category
cards.why: Always use the airplane's own checklist from the POH/AFM.

cards.q: Which approach and landing objective is assured when the pilot remains on the proper glidepath of the VASI?
c: Safe obstruction clearance in the approach area
Course guidance from the visual descent point to touchdown
Continuation of course guidance after transition to VFR
cards.why: A VASI gives vertical guidance only, with no course guidance. It guarantees obstruction clearance within ±10° of the extended centerline, out to 4 NM.

cards.q: The use of flaps in slow flight:
c: Lowers the stall speed so the airplane can fly slower, and adds drag so more power is needed
Has no effect on stall speed but reduces drag
cards.why: Flaps increase lift and drag. The bottom of the white arc (VS0) is lower than the bottom of the green arc (VS1). Expect a lower pitch attitude and more power.
cards.note: Concept answer. Your Sporty's choices may be worded differently.

cards.q: What is wake turbulence?
c: Counter-rotating vortices trailing from the wingtips of an aircraft that is producing lift
Jet blast or prop wash behind an aircraft on the ground
Turbulence from wind flowing over buildings and terrain
cards.why: Wingtip vortices form whenever a wing makes lift. They're strongest behind heavy, clean, slow aircraft.

cards.orig: (Refer to figure 48) ATC instructs you to line up and wait…
cards.q: ATC instructs you to 'line up and wait.' What should you do?
c: Taxi onto the departure runway, line up, and wait for a takeoff clearance
cards.why: Line up and wait is NOT a takeoff clearance. If you've waited a while with no call, ask ATC.

cards.orig: (Refer to figures 32, 33.) With the airplane loaded as follows, what action can be taken to balance the airplane?
cards.q: (Figures 32 & 33, concept) Your loading plots forward of the CG envelope. Which action brings it back into limits?
c: Add weight aft, such as in the baggage compartment
Add fuel to the forward-most tanks
Move a rear-seat passenger to a front seat
cards.why: Add up each item's weight and moment, then plot total weight against total moment on Figure 33. If the point is forward of the envelope, move or add weight aft. The commonly circulated FAA version (front 411 lb, rear 100 lb, 44 gal in the mains) lists 'add a 100-lb weight to the baggage compartment.' Check this against your figure.
cards.note: Figure question. Redo it in Sporty's with Download All Figures.

cards.q: Which instrument(s) will become inoperative if the static vents become clogged?
cards.why: With a static blockage, the altimeter freezes, the VSI reads zero, and the airspeed indicator becomes inaccurate (low in a climb, high in a descent).

cards.q: Hazardous attitudes occur to every pilot to some degree at some time. What are some of these hazardous attitudes?
c: Antiauthority, impulsivity, invulnerability, macho, and resignation
Poor situational awareness, snap judgments, and lack of a decision-making process
cards.why: Learn each attitude with its antidote. The test often gives a scenario and asks which attitude it shows.

cards.q: The pilot in command is responsible for ensuring that each person on board
c: is briefed on how to fasten and unfasten their seat belt and shoulder harness
cards.why: Everyone must be briefed on belts and harnesses and be buckled for taxi, takeoff and landing.

cards.q: (Figure 7) The proper adjustment to make on the attitude indicator during level flight is to align the
c: miniature airplane to the horizon bar
horizon bar to the miniature airplane
cards.why: The adjustment knob moves only the miniature airplane. In straight-and-level flight, set it on the horizon bar.

cards.q: The person directly responsible for the pre-launch briefing of passengers for a flight is the
cards.why: Passenger briefings are always the PIC's responsibility.

cards.q: How many times should you key the mic on the specified frequency at a nontowered airport to turn on pilot-controlled lighting at highest intensity?
cards.why: 7 clicks = high, 5 = medium, 3 = low, all within 5 seconds. The AIM says to key 7 times first, then step down. The lights stay on about 15 minutes.
cards.note: Your Sporty's wording may differ. The 7/5/3 rule is what's tested.

cards.q: The load factor in a level, coordinated turn with 60° of bank is:
cards.why: Load factor = 1 ÷ cos(bank) = 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2 G. Stall speed rises by √2, about 41%.

cards.q: What is ground effect?
c: The result of the surface interfering with the airflow patterns around an airplane, reducing upwash, downwash, and wingtip vortices
Extra lift from air compressed between the wing and the ground
The left-turning tendency on the takeoff roll
cards.why: Within about one wingspan of the ground, induced drag drops. That's why you float when you're fast in the flare and lift off early on takeoff.

cards.q: Wingtip vortices are created only when an aircraft is
cards.why: No lift, no vortices. They start at rotation and stop at nosewheel touchdown, so plan around those two points.

cards.orig: (Refer to figure 49.) Select the proper traffic pattern and runway for landing.
cards.q: (Figure 49, concept) On a segmented circle, what does the short leg of each L-shaped traffic pattern indicator show?
c: The direction of turns in the traffic pattern for that runway
cards.why: Step 1: use the wind cone, tee or tetrahedron to find the runway most aligned with the wind. Step 2: look at that runway's L. The long leg is the runway and the short leg is the base leg, showing which way you turn.
cards.note: Figure question. Redo it in Sporty's with Download All Figures.

cards.orig: (Refer to Figure 70, area 5) In order to avoid the Livermore Airport, what minimum…
cards.q: A Class D surface area on a sectional shows [29] in a dashed blue box. To fly over it without entering, you must be
cards.why: Bracketed numbers are the Class D ceiling in hundreds of feet MSL. A minus sign before the number means 'up to but not including' that altitude.

cards.q: A heavier airplane, due to increased load, will
c: stall at a higher airspeed and need more runway to take off
cards.why: More weight needs more lift. At any speed the wing flies at a higher angle of attack, so it reaches the critical angle sooner. Every performance number gets worse.
cards.note: Concept answer. Your Sporty's choices may be worded differently.

cards.q: What is the purpose of the runway/runway hold position sign?
c: Denotes the entrance to a runway from a taxiway
Denotes the area protected for an aircraft approaching or departing a runway
cards.why: It's a red sign with white text like '15-33', placed on a runway where another runway crosses it. You stop there only when ATC says so (for example, LAHSO).

cards.q: Preflight action, as required for all flights away from the vicinity of an airport, shall include
c: weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives if the flight can't be completed, and any known traffic delays
the designation of an alternate airport
cards.why: Memory aid NWKRAFT: NOTAMs, Weather, Known ATC delays, Runway lengths, Alternatives, Fuel, Takeoff and landing distances.

cards.q: The angle of attack at which an airplane wing stalls will
c: remain the same regardless of gross weight
increase if the CG is moved forward
change with an increase in gross weight
cards.why: The critical angle of attack is fixed for a given wing. Weight and load factor change the stall SPEED, never the stall ANGLE.

cards.q: (Figure 19) How are Significant Weather Prognostic Charts best used by a pilot?
c: For determining areas to avoid (freezing levels and turbulence)
For analyzing current frontal activity and cloud cover
For a forecast of winds aloft
cards.why: Prog charts are forecasts of hazards. For current conditions, use METARs or the surface analysis chart. For winds, use the winds-aloft forecast (FB).

cards.q: The most effective method of scanning for other aircraft for collision avoidance during daylight hours is to use
c: a series of short, regularly spaced eye movements that bring successive areas of the sky into the central visual field
one continuous sweep from wingtip to wingtip
cards.why: Step about 10° at a time and pause about 1 second on each area, because the center of the eye sees detail best. At night, do the opposite and use off-center viewing.

cards.orig: (Refer to Figure 22, area 1) While on the ground at Sandpoint airport and planning a…
cards.q: (Figure 22, concept) An airport with field elevation 2,131 ft MSL sits inside a magenta-shaded vignette. Where does Class E airspace begin over it?
cards.why: Magenta vignette = 700 AGL. Blue vignette = 1,200 AGL. Dashed magenta = surface. Add the AGL height to field elevation to get MSL. Online versions of this Sandpoint question ask for the floor of controlled airspace (2,831 MSL). The version on your test may ask something else.
cards.note: Figure question. Redo it in Sporty's with Download All Figures.

cards.q: Question 46

cards.orig: (Refer to Figure 71, area 8.) You have a flight planned from Auburn airport (AUN)…
cards.q: (Figure 71, area 8) Flight planned from Auburn (AUN)

(Figures 32 & 33) After landing, the front passenger (180 lb) gets out and a rear passenger (204 lb) moves into the vacated front seat. The airplane weighed 2,690 lb with MOM/100 of 2,260 before the change. What happens to the CG?
c: The CG moves forward approximately 3 inches
The weight changes but the CG is not affected
The CG moves forward approximately 0.1 inch
cards.why: Arms: front seats 85 in, rear seats 121 in. Old CG = 226,000 ÷ 2,690 = 84.0 in. Remove 180 × 85 = −15,300. Move 204 lb forward 36 in = −7,344. New CG = 203,356 ÷ 2,510 = 81.0 in. That's about 3 in forward.
cards.note: Check this against the figure. The math assumes Figure 32's standard arms.

cards.q: In which type of airspace are VFR flights prohibited?
cards.why: Class A runs from 18,000 ft MSL to FL600 and is IFR only. VFR flight in Class B is allowed with an ATC clearance.

cards.q: What is one flight instrument a pilot can adjust in the cockpit?
c: The altimeter (by setting the Kollsman window)
cards.why: The heading indicator (realign it with the compass) and the attitude indicator's miniature airplane are also pilot-adjustable. The airspeed indicator and VSI are not.
cards.note: If your choices listed the heading indicator instead, that's also pilot-adjustable.

cards.q: Wingtip vortices created by large aircraft tend to
c: sink below the aircraft generating them
rise into the takeoff or landing path of a crossing runway
cards.why: They sink 300 to 500 fpm and level off 500 to 1,000 ft below the flight path. Near the ground they drift outward at 2 to 3 kt.

cards.q: On final approach to a runway with a standard 2-bar VASI, red over white means you are
cards.why: Red over white, you're all right. White over white, you're too high. Red over red, you're too low.

cards.q: When landing behind a large aircraft, which procedure should you follow?
c: Stay at or above its final approach flightpath and land beyond its touchdown point
Stay below its flightpath and land before its touchdown point
Stay below its flightpath and land beyond its touchdown point
cards.why: Vortices sink, so stay high. They stop when the wing stops making lift, so land past its touchdown point. When taking off behind one, lift off before its rotation point and climb above its path.

cards.q: While operating in Class D airspace, each pilot of an aircraft approaching to land on a runway served by a VASI shall
c: maintain an altitude at or above the glide slope until a lower altitude is necessary for a safe landing
maintain an altitude at or below the glide slope
stay on the glide slope until 50 ft above the threshold
cards.why: This is a regulation, not just advice.

cards.q: Why should you establish a nose-high pitch attitude during the takeoff roll on a soft field?
c: To get the weight off the nosewheel as soon as possible and lift off at the lowest airspeed
To improve visibility over the nose
cards.why: Less weight on the wheels means less drag from mud, snow or grass. After liftoff, stay in ground effect to accelerate before climbing.

cards.orig: (Refer to figure 62.) In flying the rectangular course shown, when would the aircraft be…
cards.q: (Figure 62, concept) Flying a rectangular course in wind, which turns will be less than 90°?
c: The turns onto and off the upwind leg
The turns onto and off the downwind leg
cards.why: You crab into the wind on the crosswind legs, so your heading already points partly upwind. The upwind-end turns are less than 90° with the shallowest bank (slowest groundspeed). The downwind-end turns are more than 90° with the steepest bank.
cards.note: Figure question. Apply this rule to the figure's numbered corners.

cards.q: If you are on a cross-country flight, to keep from losing your course you should:
c: Fly a wind-corrected heading and check your position against charted checkpoints regularly
Fly toward your destination's beacon only
cards.why: Pilotage plus dead reckoning: put a checkpoint every 10 to 20 NM, note your time at each, and correct drift early. If you get lost: Climb, Communicate, Confess, Comply, Conserve.
cards.note: Concept answer. Your Sporty's choices may be worded differently.

cards.q: Stall speed is increased by:
c: increased load factor, such as in a steep turn
cards.why: Stall speed goes UP with load factor, weight, a forward CG, and ice or frost. It goes DOWN with flaps and lighter weight.

cards.q: If you face an emergency where you want ATC assistance but are not already in contact with ATC, what should you do?
cards.why: Codes: 7700 = emergency, 7600 = lost communications, 7500 = hijack, 1200 = VFR. 121.5 MHz is the emergency frequency.

cards.q: (Figure 25, area 3) Dallas
What is required to enter Class B airspace?
c: An ATC clearance, two-way radio, a Mode C transponder, and ADS-B Out
cards.why: ATC must actually say 'cleared into the Class Bravo.' You also need a private pilot certificate, or a student pilot certificate with the specific endorsement.

cards.q: What is required to enter Class C airspace?
c: Two-way radio communication established with ATC before entering
cards.why: If the controller answers using your call sign, communication is established. 'Aircraft calling, standby' does not count. Typical size: 5 NM core from the surface to 4,000 AGL, and a 10 NM shelf from 1,200 to 4,000 AGL.

cards.q: VFR weather minimums in Class B airspace
c: 3 SM, 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal
cards.why: Class B is the only controlled airspace with 'clear of clouds' as the cloud clearance.

cards.q: VFR weather minimums in Class C, D and E airspace below 10,000 ft MSL
c: 3 SM; 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal from clouds
5 SM; 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 1 SM horizontal
cards.why: Memory aid '3-152': 3 SM visibility; 1,000 above, 500 below, 2,000 horizontal.

cards.q: VFR weather minimums at or above 10,000 ft MSL (more than 1,200 ft AGL)
c: 5 SM; 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 1 SM horizontal
3 SM; 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal
cards.why: Higher altitude means faster airplanes, so the minimums are bigger.

cards.q: Class G airspace, day, at or below 1,200 ft AGL: VFR minimums?
c: 1 SM; 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal
cards.why: At night in the same airspace: 3 SM and 500/1,000/2,000. Exception: in a traffic pattern within ½ mile of the runway, 1 SM and clear of clouds.

cards.q: Class G airspace, day, above 1,200 ft AGL but below 10,000 ft MSL: minimum flight visibility?
c: 1 SM (with 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal from clouds)
cards.why: The visibility stays at 1 SM but the cloud clearance increases above 1,200 AGL.

cards.q: Maximum indicated airspeed below 10,000 ft MSL
cards.why: 200 kt applies under a Class B shelf, in a VFR corridor, and at or below 2,500 AGL within 4 NM of the primary airport of Class C or D airspace.

cards.q: Minimum safe altitude over a congested area (city, town, or settlement)
c: 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft horizontally
cards.why: Non-congested areas: 500 ft above the surface. Open water or sparse areas: no closer than 500 ft to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure. Anywhere: high enough for a safe emergency landing.

cards.q: VFR cruising altitude for a magnetic course of 090° (more than 3,000 ft AGL)
cards.why: Courses 0–179° magnetic: odd + 500. Courses 180–359°: even + 500. The rule uses magnetic COURSE, not heading.

cards.q: After drinking alcohol, how long must you wait before acting as a crewmember?
c: 8 hours, and blood alcohol must be below 0.04%
cards.why: Remember '8 hours bottle to throttle' and 0.04%.

cards.q: To carry passengers, what landing currency do you need?
c: 3 takeoffs and landings in the preceding 90 days, in the same category and class
cards.why: For night passengers: 3 to a FULL STOP between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise. Tailwheel airplanes always need full stops.

cards.q: How often is a flight review required?
cards.why: It includes at least 1 hour of ground and 1 hour of flight training.

cards.q: Minimum VFR fuel reserve, at normal cruise speed
cards.why: It's fuel to reach your first point of intended landing plus the reserve.

cards.q: When must the required flight crew use supplemental oxygen?
c: From 12,500 to 14,000 ft MSL for more than 30 minutes, and at all times above 14,000 ft
cards.why: Above 15,000 ft MSL, every passenger must be PROVIDED with oxygen.

cards.q: Which documents must be on board? (ARROW)
c: Airworthiness certificate, Registration, Radio station license (if flying internationally), Operating limitations, Weight & balance data
cards.why: Your pilot certificate, medical (or BasicMed), and photo ID go with you, not the airplane.

cards.q: Required inspection intervals
c: Annual every 12 calendar months; transponder every 24; ELT every 12; 100-hour if the airplane is used for hire
Only an annual is ever required
cards.why: Memory aid AV1ATE: Airworthiness directives, VOR check (IFR, 30 days), 100-hour, Annual, Transponder, ELT.

cards.q: An accident with substantial damage must be reported to the NTSB
cards.why: Notify immediately. The written report is due within 10 days.

cards.q: Two airplanes are converging at about the same altitude (not head-on). Who has the right-of-way?
cards.why: An aircraft in distress has right-of-way over everyone. Then balloon > glider > airship > airplane/rotorcraft. Head-on: both turn right. Overtaking: pass on the right. Landing: the lower aircraft has right-of-way.

cards.q: Prohibited area vs. restricted area vs. MOA
c: Prohibited: no flight. Restricted: permission needed when active. MOA: VFR allowed, use extreme caution
All three ban flight at all times
An MOA needs a clearance; a restricted area doesn't
cards.why: Warning areas are like restricted areas but over international waters. Alert areas mean heavy training traffic.

cards.q: Special VFR in a Class B, C, D or E surface area requires
c: An ATC clearance, 1 SM visibility, and staying clear of clouds (at night: instrument rating and an IFR-equipped airplane)
3 SM visibility and clear of clouds
cards.why: It's only available below 10,000 ft MSL.

cards.q: In a METAR, what is the ceiling?
c: The lowest broken (BKN) or overcast (OVC) layer, or vertical visibility (VV)
The lowest layer of any coverage
cards.why: Heights are in hundreds of feet AGL, so BKN015 = broken at 1,500 ft. FEW and SCT layers are never ceilings.

cards.q: What three conditions are needed for a thunderstorm to form?
c: Sufficient moisture, an unstable lapse rate, and a lifting force
Stable air, high humidity, and calm wind
Cold air over warm water only
cards.why: Life cycle: cumulus (updrafts), mature (rain reaches the ground, strongest up- and downdrafts), dissipating (downdrafts).

cards.q: Characteristics of stable air
c: Stratiform clouds, smooth air, poor visibility, steady precipitation
Cumuliform clouds, turbulence, good visibility, showery precipitation
cards.why: Unstable air is the exact opposite. The test likes to swap the two.

cards.q: Advection fog forms when
c: moist air moves over a colder surface, often along coasts, and it needs wind
the ground cools on clear, calm nights
moist, stable air is pushed up sloping terrain
cards.why: Radiation fog forms on clear, calm nights in low areas. Upslope fog forms when moist air is pushed up terrain.

cards.q: A narrowing temperature/dewpoint spread indicates
c: fog or low clouds are likely
cards.why: To estimate cloud bases: spread in °C ÷ 2.5 × 1,000 ft, or °F ÷ 4.4 × 1,000 ft.

cards.q: If you fly from warm air into colder air without resetting the altimeter, it will read
cards.why: 'High to low, look out below.' Going from high to low pressure or temperature means you're lower than the altimeter shows.

cards.q: Where is clear air turbulence most likely near the jet stream?
c: On the polar (cold) side of the jet stream
cards.why: A frequently missed one. Remember the cold side.

cards.q: Standard sea-level atmosphere and standard temperature lapse rate
c: 15 °C and 29.92 inHg; temperature drops about 2 °C (3.5 °F) per 1,000 ft
cards.why: Pressure drops about 1 inHg per 1,000 ft. 15 °C is the same as 59 °F.

cards.q: Why must frost be removed from the wings before flight?
c: It disrupts smooth airflow, reducing lift and adding drag, so the airplane may not get airborne
cards.why: Even frost as rough as sandpaper can stop a takeoff.

cards.q: Which factors increase density altitude?
c: Higher temperature, higher elevation, and higher humidity
cards.why: High density altitude means poor performance: a longer takeoff roll and a weaker climb.

cards.q: What is the pressure altitude at an airport with 1,000 ft elevation and an altimeter setting of 30.42?
cards.why: (29.92 − 30.42) × 1,000 = −500. Then 1,000 − 500 = 500 ft. A higher setting gives a lower pressure altitude.

cards.q: What are the four left-turning tendencies?
c: Torque, P-factor, spiraling slipstream, and gyroscopic precession
Torque, adverse yaw, ground effect, and washout
P-factor, load factor, induced drag, and skid
cards.why: P-factor is strongest at a high angle of attack with high power, as in a climb.

cards.q: How does a forward CG affect stall speed?
cards.why: The tail has to push down harder, so the wing carries extra load. A forward CG is more stable but makes the flare harder. An aft CG is less stable and makes stall and spin recovery harder.

cards.q: What causes an airplane to turn?
cards.why: Banking tilts the lift vector to the side. The rudder only keeps the turn coordinated.

cards.q: How is adverse yaw corrected?
c: Rudder in the direction of the turn
cards.why: The down aileron on the rising wing adds lift AND drag, which yaws the nose away from the turn.

cards.q: Washout on a wing is
c: Angle of incidence decreasing from root to tip, so the root stalls first
Chord decreasing from root to tip
Angle of incidence increasing from root to tip
cards.why: The wingtips keep flying, so the ailerons still work in a stall.

cards.q: What happens to maneuvering speed (Va) when the airplane's weight decreases?
cards.why: A lighter airplane is pushed around more easily by gusts, so it must slow down more to protect the structure.

cards.q: As airspeed increases in level flight, induced drag
cards.why: Parasite drag rises with speed. Induced drag is highest at low speed and high angle of attack.

cards.q: In a skidding turn, the
c: ball is to the outside of the turn: too much rudder for the bank
ball is to the inside of the turn: too little rudder
cards.why: A slip is the opposite: the ball is inside the turn. In either case, 'step on the ball.'

cards.q: When is carburetor ice most likely, and what's the first sign with a fixed-pitch propeller?
c: Between about 20 °F and 70 °F with high humidity; first sign is a loss of RPM
Only below freezing; first sign is a rise in oil temperature
Only in visible rain; first sign is engine roughness
cards.why: Applying carb heat drops the RPM further (warm air enriches the mixture). If ice was there, the RPM then gradually rises.

cards.q: Detonation vs. preignition
c: Detonation: the fuel explodes instead of burning evenly (low-grade fuel, too lean, too hot). Preignition: the fuel ignites early from a hot spot
Detonation is caused by a fuel mixture that is too rich
cards.why: If you suspect detonation, enrich the mixture, lower the nose to cool the engine, and reduce power.

cards.q: Magnetic compass errors in the Northern Hemisphere
c: ANDS: Accelerate North, Decelerate South (on east or west headings). UNOS: Undershoot North, Overshoot South when turning
The compass is accurate during turns
Acceleration shows a turn to the south
cards.why: These errors are why you realign the heading indicator only in straight, level, unaccelerated flight.

cards.q: Airspeed indicator markings
c: White arc: flap range (bottom = VS0). Green: normal range (bottom = VS1, top = VNO). Yellow: caution, smooth air only. Red line: VNE
Green: flap range. White: normal range
cards.why: Expect a question that asks you to read one of these from a figure.

cards.q: What is calibrated airspeed?
c: Indicated airspeed corrected for instrument and position error
Indicated airspeed corrected for altitude and temperature
cards.why: True airspeed is calibrated airspeed corrected for altitude and temperature.

cards.q: Which instruments are gyroscopic, and what powers them in a typical trainer?
c: Attitude and heading indicators (vacuum); turn coordinator (electric)
cards.why: If the vacuum system fails, the turn coordinator still works.

cards.q: Light gun signals to an aircraft ON THE GROUND
c: Steady green: cleared for takeoff. Flashing green: cleared to taxi. Steady red: stop. Flashing red: taxi clear of the runway in use. Flashing white: return to starting point
Steady green: taxi. Flashing green: takeoff. Steady red: taxi clear
Flashing red: stop. Steady red: return to starting point
cards.why: Alternating red and green means exercise extreme caution, both on the ground and in flight.

cards.q: Light gun signals to an aircraft IN FLIGHT
c: Steady green: cleared to land. Flashing green: return for landing. Steady red: give way and keep circling. Flashing red: airport unsafe, do not land
Steady red: airport unsafe. Flashing red: give way and circle
cards.why: The steady red vs. flashing red difference is one of the most missed items.

cards.q: What does a civilian land airport's rotating beacon flash?
cards.why: Two whites then green = military field. Yellow = water airport. A beacon on in daylight in Class B, C, D or E surface areas can mean below-VFR weather (ceiling under 1,000 ft or visibility under 3 SM).

cards.q: On the pavement before a displaced threshold (white arrows), you may
c: taxi, take off, and roll out after landing, but not touch down
cards.why: Yellow chevrons mark a blast pad or stopway, which can't be used for anything.

cards.q: Airport sign colors
c: Red with white text: mandatory (hold here). Black with yellow text: location. Yellow with black text: direction or destination
Yellow with black text: mandatory. Red with white text: location
cards.why: If a sign is red, you need ATC permission to go past it.

cards.q: At runway hold-short markings, which side do you stop on?
c: The side with the two SOLID yellow lines
The side with the two dashed lines
cards.why: Solid lines facing you mean stop. Dashed lines facing you mean you can cross them when exiting the runway.

cards.q: If ATIS doesn't mention sky condition or visibility, it means
c: the ceiling is at least 5,000 ft and visibility is 5 SM or more
the sky is clear and visibility is unrestricted
the weather is at or above VFR minimums
cards.why: Remember '5 and 5.'

cards.q: Transponder codes to know
cards.why: Memory aid: 75 taken alive, 76 radio fix, 77 going to heaven.

cards.q: Checking a VOR receiver with a VOT: with the CDI centered, the OBS and TO/FROM should read
c: 0° FROM or 180° TO, regardless of your position
180° FROM, only if you are due north of the VOT
0° TO or 180° FROM, regardless of your position
cards.why: A VOT broadcasts the 360 radial in every direction. Allowed error is ±4°.

cards.q: How far will you travel in 14.5 minutes at a groundspeed of 98 knots?
cards.why: Distance = groundspeed × minutes ÷ 60 = 98 × 14.5 ÷ 60 = 23.7 NM.

cards.q: How long will it take to fly 35 NM at a groundspeed of 105 knots?
cards.why: 35 ÷ 105 = 0.333 hr × 60 = 20 min. Watch for distractor numbers in these questions.

cards.q: To convert a true course to a magnetic course with 10° EAST variation, you
cards.why: East is least (subtract), west is best (add). Variation turns true into magnetic; deviation (from the compass card) turns magnetic into compass.

cards.q: The agonic line is where
cards.why: Isogonic lines connect points with the same variation. The agonic line is the 0° isogonic line.

cards.q: What distance does DME display?
c: Horizontal ground distance in statute miles
cards.why: Directly over the station at 6,000 ft, DME reads about 1 NM.

cards.q: How is each airspace class drawn on a sectional?
c: Class B: solid blue. Class C: solid magenta. Class D: dashed blue. Class E surface area: dashed magenta
Class B: dashed blue. Class D: solid blue
cards.why: Shelves and ceilings are shown in hundreds of feet MSL.

cards.q: If you become lost, your first step should be to
c: climb for better visibility and radio/nav reception, then orient yourself
descend for a better look at landmarks
cards.why: The 5 Cs: Climb, Communicate, Confess, Comply, Conserve fuel.
cards.ref: Airplane Flying Handbook · Rotate Pilot most-missed

cards.q: Hypemic hypoxia is caused by
c: the blood's reduced ability to carry oxygen, such as from carbon monoxide or anemia
high altitude (low partial pressure of oxygen)
cards.why: Hypoxic = altitude. Hypemic = blood. Stagnant = poor circulation. Histotoxic = cells can't use oxygen (alcohol, drugs).

cards.q: Hyperventilation is best treated by
c: slowing your breathing rate, talking aloud, or breathing into a bag
cards.why: The symptoms look like hypoxia. If you're not sure which it is, check your oxygen first.

cards.q: An upsloping runway, a narrower-than-usual runway, or rain on the windscreen creates the illusion of being
c: higher than you actually are, so you fly a lower approach
lower than you actually are, so you fly too high
farther away than you actually are
cards.why: A wide or downsloping runway does the opposite: you think you're low, so you fly too high. Haze makes the runway look farther away.

cards.q: What does the DECIDE model stand for?
c: Detect, Estimate, Choose, Identify, Do, Evaluate
Determine, Estimate, Choose, Investigate, Decide, Evaluate
Detect, Evaluate, Choose, Implement, Document, End
cards.why: Also know IMSAFE (Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion) and PAVE (Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, External pressures).

cards.q: How long do your eyes take to fully adapt to darkness?
cards.why: Avoid bright white light before a night flight. It resets the adaptation.

cards.q: What is the antidote for the hazardous attitude 'Invulnerability'?
cards.why: 'Follow the rules' = antiauthority. 'Not so fast' = impulsivity. 'Taking chances is foolish' = macho. 'I'm not helpless' = resignation.

cards.q: If you suspect carbon monoxide poisoning (headache, drowsiness, dizziness), you should
c: shut off the cabin heater, open the fresh-air vents, and use oxygen if available
cards.why: Carbon monoxide usually leaks from the exhaust-shroud heater. It causes hypemic hypoxia.

cards.q: On a windsock (wind cone), which way is the wind blowing?
c: From the large open end toward the small end: the open end faces into the wind
From the small end toward the open end
The windsock shows only wind speed
cards.why: The wind blows into the big end, so the sock streams downwind. A fully extended sock usually means about 15 kt or more.

cards.q: A LAHSO clearance means you must
c: land and stop before a specified intersecting runway or point; the pilot in command may decline it
hold short of the runway before departure
cards.why: Land And Hold Short Operations. Accept only if you can stop in the available landing distance. You can always say 'unable'.

cards.q: Taxiing with a quartering headwind from the left, how should you hold the controls?
c: Yoke turned left (left aileron up), elevator neutral
Yoke turned right (left aileron down), elevator forward
cards.why: Headwind: 'climb into the wind' (aileron up on the upwind side). Tailwind: 'dive away from the wind' (aileron down on the upwind side, elevator forward).

cards.q: Taxiing with a quartering tailwind from the left, how should you hold the controls?
c: Yoke turned right (left aileron down) and yoke forward (elevator down)
Yoke turned left and full back elevator
cards.why: Dive away from the wind: this keeps the tailwind from lifting the upwind wing and the tail.

cards.q: What are runway end identifier lights (REIL)?
c: A pair of synchronized flashing lights at the threshold that identify the runway end
Red lights at the far end of the runway
cards.why: They help you pick out the approach end of a runway against surrounding lights.

cards.q: What color are taxiway lead-off lights leaving a runway?
cards.why: Taxiway edge lights are blue, taxiway centerline lights are green, and lead-off lights alternate green and yellow.

cards.q: As a private pilot, what may you accept from passengers?
c: A pro-rata share of the fuel, oil, airport fees or rental cost
Any amount, as long as you don't make a profit
Nothing: private pilots may not accept any money
cards.why: 14 CFR 61.113(c): you must pay at least your equal share of the operating expenses.

cards.q: Which flight time must be recorded in a pilot logbook?
c: Training and experience used to meet requirements for a certificate, rating, flight review or recency
cards.why: You only have to log what you use to meet a requirement, though most pilots log everything.

cards.q: For private pilot privileges, a third-class medical issued to a pilot under 40 is valid until
c: the end of the 60th calendar month after the exam
the end of the 24th calendar month after the exam
the end of the 12th calendar month after the exam
cards.why: Age 40 or older at the exam: 24 calendar months. BasicMed is an alternative for many pilots.

cards.q: When must the airplane's position (nav) lights be on?
c: From one hour after sunset to one hour before sunrise
cards.why: Don't confuse this with passenger currency at night, which runs from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise.

cards.q: Night flight time that may be logged is the time between
c: the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight
one hour after sunset and one hour before sunrise
cards.why: Three different 'night' definitions are tested: lights (sunset), logging (civil twilight), and passenger currency (1 hour after sunset).

cards.q: Aerobatic flight is prohibited below what altitude?
cards.why: It's also prohibited over congested areas, in Class B/C/D/E surface areas, within 4 NM of a federal airway centerline, or with flight visibility under 3 SM.

cards.q: With a passenger aboard, parachutes are required for any intentional maneuver exceeding
c: 60° of bank or 30° nose-up or nose-down
cards.why: Exceptions include flight tests and training by a CFI for a certificate or rating (spins, for example).

cards.q: Where do you find Temporary Flight Restrictions (TFRs)?
c: In FDC NOTAMs (check before every flight)
cards.why: TFRs pop up for VIP movement, wildfires, stadium events and more. Always check NOTAMs in your preflight briefing.

cards.q: A Military Training Route labelled IR or VR with four digits (e.g., VR1234) is flown
cards.why: Three digits means at least one segment is above 1,500 ft AGL. These are fast, low-flying military jets.

cards.q: Who is responsible for determining whether the airplane is in condition for safe flight?
c: The mechanic who signed the last inspection
cards.why: The PIC must not start a flight in an unairworthy airplane.

cards.q: When may an ELT be tested?
c: During the first 5 minutes after the hour, for no more than three audio sweeps
At any time, for up to 1 minute
cards.why: Testing outside that window can trigger a real search.

cards.q: After changing your permanent mailing address, you may keep exercising pilot privileges for only
c: 30 days unless you notify the FAA
cards.why: Update your address with the FAA Airmen Certification Branch (or in IACRA).

cards.q: How far does the Mode C veil extend from a Class B primary airport?
c: 30 NM, from the surface to 10,000 ft MSL
cards.why: Inside it you need an altitude-reporting transponder and ADS-B Out.

cards.q: A TAF covers what area?
c: Within 5 statute miles of the centre of the airport's runway complex
cards.why: TAFs are usually valid for 24 hours (30 at some large airports) and use the same codes as METARs.

cards.q: Which AIRMET covers turbulence, strong surface winds and low-level wind shear?
cards.why: Sierra = IFR and mountain obscuration. Tango = turbulence. Zulu = icing and freezing levels.

cards.q: A non-convective SIGMET is issued for
c: severe icing, severe or extreme turbulence, dust or sandstorms below 3 SM visibility, and volcanic ash
IFR conditions over a large area
cards.why: Convective SIGMETs cover thunderstorms. SIGMET hazards matter to every airplane, not just small ones.

cards.q: A PIREP coded UUA is
cards.why: UA = routine, UUA = urgent (severe turbulence or icing, wind shear, volcanic ash, and so on).

cards.q: Ice pellets (sleet) at the surface tell you
c: there is freezing rain at a higher altitude
the air aloft is colder than at the surface
cards.why: Rain falls from warmer air above and freezes into pellets on the way down. Freezing rain is the fastest way to build clear ice.

cards.q: Which clouds have the greatest turbulence?
cards.why: Thunderstorms can contain severe turbulence, hail, lightning and wind shear. Stay at least 20 NM away.

cards.q: Where can you expect low-level wind shear?
c: In a low-level temperature inversion, near thunderstorms and in frontal zones
cards.why: Sudden airspeed changes during takeoff or landing are the danger.

cards.q: Stationary lens-shaped (lenticular) clouds downwind of mountains indicate
c: mountain waves and possible strong turbulence
cards.why: Standing lenticulars mean strong winds over the ridge. Expect up- and downdrafts and rotor turbulence.

cards.q: What causes the variations in altimeter settings between weather stations?
c: Unequal heating of the Earth's surface
cards.why: Uneven heating creates pressure differences, which is why you update your altimeter along the route.

cards.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, wind circulates around a high-pressure area
cards.why: Highs turn clockwise, outward and descending (usually fair weather). Lows turn counterclockwise, inward and rising (clouds and weather).

cards.q: Which VOR indications mean you are on the 030 radial?
c: OBS 030 with FROM centred, or OBS 210 with TO centred
cards.why: Radials always point away from the station. The 030 radial is northeast of the VOR.

cards.q: Magnetic compass deviation is
c: error caused by magnetic fields inside the airplane, shown on the compass correction card
the angle between true and magnetic north
cards.why: Variation is the difference between true and magnetic north. Deviation is the airplane's own error.

cards.q: How should you measure a true course on a sectional chart?
c: Measure from a meridian near the midpoint of the course line
Measure from the nearest isogonic line
Measure from the top edge of the chart
cards.why: Meridians converge toward the pole, so the midpoint gives the most accurate average course.

cards.q: One nautical mile is about
cards.why: Knots are nautical miles per hour. Visibility is in statute miles.

cards.q: If the wind is from the right of your course, you should
c: turn your heading to the right of the course (crab into the wind)
turn your heading to the left of the course
keep the heading equal to the course
cards.why: Crab into the wind. Add the wind correction angle for a wind from the right; subtract it for one from the left.

cards.q: Lines of latitude
c: run east–west and measure position north or south of the equator
run north–south and measure position east or west of Greenwich
connect points of equal magnetic variation
cards.why: Lines of longitude (meridians) run north–south. Isogonic lines connect points of equal variation.

cards.q: Which left-turning tendency is strongest at high power and a high angle of attack?
cards.why: The descending blade takes a bigger bite than the ascending one, so you need right rudder in a climb.

cards.q: Pitch is movement about which axis?
cards.why: Roll is about the longitudinal axis (ailerons). Yaw is about the vertical axis (rudder).

cards.q: At a high density altitude, the indicated airspeed at which the airplane stalls
c: stays the same, but true airspeed and groundspeed at the stall are higher
cards.why: So fly the same indicated speeds, but expect longer takeoff and landing rolls.

cards.q: When you trim nose-up, the elevator trim tab
c: moves down, which pushes the elevator up
stays neutral while the stabilizer moves
cards.why: Trim tabs move opposite to the control surface they hold.

cards.q: What color is 100LL avgas?
cards.why: Jet A is clear or straw-coloured. Misfuelling with the wrong type is a deadly risk.

cards.q: Using fuel with a lower grade than specified is most likely to cause
cards.why: Detonation can damage pistons quickly. Use only the grades listed in the POH.

cards.q: With a fixed-pitch propeller, the main power indication is the
cards.why: A constant-speed propeller uses manifold pressure for power and RPM for propeller speed.

cards.q: An abnormally high oil temperature may be caused by
c: an oil level that is too low
cards.why: Other causes: a too-lean mixture, high power at low airspeed (long climbs), and detonation.

cards.q: After an alternator failure, the electrical system runs on
c: the battery alone for a limited time, so shed electrical load
cards.why: The magnetos keep the engine running, but they don't power the electrical bus.

cards.q: In the IMSAFE checklist, the 'E' stands for
cards.why: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion/Eating: a personal fitness check before every flight.

cards.q: What does the PAVE checklist stand for?
cards.why: Use it during preflight planning to spot risk factors.

cards.q: The 'leans' illusion is caused by
c: an abrupt correction after a slow, unnoticed roll, making you feel banked the other way
staring at a stationary light at night
cards.why: Trust the attitude indicator. Your inner ear can't sense slow rolls.

cards.q: After a recreational scuba dive that did not require a controlled ascent, how long should you wait before flying up to 8,000 ft MSL?
cards.why: Wait 24 hours after a dive that required a controlled ascent, and before any flight above 8,000 ft.

cards.q: Spatial disorientation is most likely when
c: outside visual references are lost, such as in cloud or on a dark night
the airplane is in coordinated flight
cards.why: VFR pilots who fly into cloud often lose control within minutes. Turn back early.

cards.q: How long is a third-class medical certificate valid for private pilot privileges if you were under 40 on the date of the exam?
cards.why: Under 40 on the exam date: 60 calendar months. Age 40 or older: 24 calendar months.

cards.q: A pilot who was 45 when she passed a third-class medical exam may use it for private pilot privileges until
c: the end of the 24th month after the month of the exam
the end of the 60th month after the month of the exam
the end of the 12th month after the month of the exam
cards.why: At 40 or older, a third-class medical lasts 24 calendar months, ending on the last day of the 24th month.

cards.q: A second-class medical certificate issued to a 30-year-old is good for private pilot privileges for
cards.why: A second-class medical is valid for commercial privileges for 12 months, then reverts to third-class privileges for the rest of the third-class period.

cards.q: To act as pilot in command, a private pilot must have completed a flight review within the preceding
cards.why: A flight review is at least 1 hour of flight training and 1 hour of ground training, every 24 calendar months.

cards.q: What is the minimum content of a flight review?
c: 1 hour of ground training and 1 hour of flight training
3 takeoffs and landings to a full stop
cards.why: At least 1 hour of ground training (Part 91 rules and procedures) and 1 hour of flight training, with a logbook endorsement.

cards.q: To carry passengers at night, the three required takeoffs and landings must have been
c: to a full stop, between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise
to a full stop, during civil twilight
cards.why: Night passenger currency needs three full-stop takeoffs and landings in the night period defined as 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise, within 90 days.

cards.q: For tailwheel airplanes, the three takeoffs and landings needed to carry passengers must be
cards.why: Tailwheel currency requires full-stop landings.

cards.q: What must a pilot have in their physical possession when acting as pilot in command?
c: A pilot certificate, a medical certificate (or BasicMed documents) and photo identification
A pilot certificate and the logbook
cards.why: You need the pilot certificate, a medical certificate if one is required, and government photo ID such as a driver's license.

cards.q: A private pilot may share the operating expenses of a flight with passengers, provided the pilot pays
c: at least an equal (pro rata) share of fuel, oil, airport expenditures or rental fees
nothing, as long as the passengers are friends
at least half the total cost regardless of how many passengers
cards.why: Private pilots may not pay less than the pro rata share of fuel, oil, airport expenditures or rental fees.

cards.q: A private pilot may act as pilot in command for compensation
c: only when the flight is incidental to a business or employment and no passengers or property are carried for compensation
whenever the pilot has more than 200 hours
cards.why: The business-incidental exception allows it if the flight is only incidental to the business and carries no passengers or property for compensation or hire.

cards.q: To act as pilot in command of a high-performance airplane, you need a one-time endorsement if its engine produces more than
cards.why: High performance means an engine of more than 200 horsepower.

cards.q: A complex airplane is one with
c: retractable landing gear, flaps and a controllable-pitch propeller (or FADEC)
a tailwheel and a constant-speed propeller
cards.why: Complex means retractable gear, flaps and a controllable-pitch propeller, or an engine controlled by FADEC.

cards.q: A student pilot may not carry passengers and may not fly solo in daytime when the flight visibility is less than
cards.why: Student solo flight requires at least 3 SM flight visibility by day and 5 SM at night, with visual reference to the surface.

cards.q: A student pilot's solo flight endorsement must have been made within the preceding
cards.why: The solo endorsement in the logbook must be dated within the 90 days before the flight.

cards.q: After an alcohol-related motor vehicle action, a pilot must send a written report to the FAA Security and Investigations Division within
cards.why: Each motor vehicle action involving alcohol or drugs must be reported within 60 days.

cards.q: What is the minimum time that must pass after drinking alcohol before you may act as a crewmember?
cards.why: No flying within 8 hours of drinking alcohol, while under the influence, or with a blood alcohol concentration of 0.04 or more.

cards.q: You may not act as a crewmember with a blood alcohol concentration of
cards.why: The limit is below 0.04 by weight. Many pilots use a stricter personal rule: 12 to 24 hours, not 8.

cards.q: Who is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of an aircraft?
cards.why: The pilot in command is the final authority, and may deviate from any rule in an emergency to the extent needed.

cards.q: If you deviate from a rule during an in-flight emergency, the FAA may ask for a written report. You must send it
c: within 10 days, even if not requested
only if ATC gave you priority
cards.why: A PIC who deviates in an emergency sends a written report if the Administrator requests one.

cards.q: Before every flight, the pilot in command must become familiar with all available information. For a flight away from the vicinity of an airport this must include
c: weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives if the flight can't be completed, and known ATC delays
the aircraft maintenance records for the past year
cards.why: Preflight action includes weather, fuel requirements, alternatives and known traffic delays, plus runway lengths and takeoff and landing distance data.

cards.q: For every flight, the preflight action required by regulation includes
c: runway lengths at the airports of intended use and takeoff and landing distance data
getting a standard briefing from Flight Service
cards.why: Runway lengths and takeoff and landing distance information are required for every flight, not only cross-countries.

cards.q: On a day VFR flight, an airplane must carry enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and then, at normal cruise speed, for at least
cards.why: Day VFR: 30 minutes of reserve fuel at normal cruising speed. Night VFR: 45 minutes.

cards.q: Which people must wear a safety belt during taxi, takeoff and landing?
c: Each person on board (a child under 2 may be held by an adult)
cards.why: Each person must occupy a seat with a safety belt fastened for movement on the surface, takeoff and landing. The PIC must brief passengers on how to use them.

cards.q: No pilot may drop an object from an aircraft in flight
c: that creates a hazard to persons or property
unless they have a waiver from ATC
cards.why: Dropping objects is allowed if reasonable precautions are taken to avoid injury or damage.

cards.q: Two aircraft are approaching each other head-on. What should each pilot do?
c: The higher aircraft climbs and the lower one descends
cards.why: In a head-on approach, each pilot alters course to the right.

cards.q: An airplane is overtaking another airplane. Which way should the overtaking pilot pass?
cards.why: The aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way; the overtaking aircraft passes well clear on the right.

cards.q: Which aircraft has the right-of-way over all other air traffic?
cards.why: An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic.

cards.q: An airplane and a glider are converging. Which has the right-of-way?
cards.why: Less maneuverable aircraft have priority: balloon, then glider, then airship, then airplane and rotorcraft.

cards.q: Two aircraft are approaching to land. Which has the right-of-way?
c: The aircraft at the lower altitude, though it may not cut in front of another aircraft on final
The aircraft at the higher altitude
cards.why: The lower aircraft has the right-of-way but may not take advantage of that to cut in front of or overtake another.

cards.q: Over a sparsely populated area, except for takeoff and landing, an airplane may not be operated closer than
c: 500 ft to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure
500 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft
cards.why: Over open water or sparsely populated areas, stay at least 500 ft from any person, vessel, vehicle or structure.

cards.q: Anywhere, the minimum altitude rule requires an altitude that allows
c: an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property on the surface if a power unit fails
a glide to the nearest airport
at least 500 ft of terrain clearance at all times
cards.why: Everywhere: an altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to people or property below.

cards.q: VFR cruising more than 3,000 ft AGL on a magnetic course of 090°, which altitude is appropriate?
c: Odd thousands plus 500 ft, such as 5,500
Even thousands plus 500 ft, such as 6,500
cards.why: Magnetic courses 0° to 179°: odd thousands plus 500 ft. 180° to 359°: even thousands plus 500 ft.

cards.q: VFR cruising above 3,000 ft AGL on a magnetic course of 270°, you should fly at
c: even thousands plus 500 ft, such as 4,500
odd thousands plus 500 ft, such as 5,500
cards.why: Westbound (180° to 359° magnetic course): even thousands plus 500 ft.

cards.q: The VFR cruising altitude rule is based on
cards.why: It's based on magnetic course, not heading, and applies above 3,000 ft AGL.

cards.q: Below 10,000 ft MSL, the maximum indicated airspeed is
cards.why: 250 KIAS below 10,000 ft MSL, unless authorized.

cards.q: At or below 2,500 ft above the surface within 4 NM of the primary airport of a Class C or D airspace area, the maximum indicated airspeed is
cards.why: 200 KIAS within 4 NM of the primary airport of Class C or D, at or below 2,500 ft AGL, unless authorized.

cards.q: Flying beneath the lateral limits of Class B airspace, the maximum indicated airspeed is
cards.why: Under a Class B shelf or in a VFR corridor through Class B: 200 KIAS.

cards.q: Aerobatic flight is not allowed when the flight visibility is less than
cards.why: Aerobatics need at least 3 SM flight visibility.

cards.q: No person may operate an aircraft in formation flight
c: except by arrangement with the pilot in command of each aircraft in the formation
unless both pilots are commercial pilots
within Class B airspace at any time
cards.why: Formation flight requires prior arrangement with each PIC, and never for hire with passengers.

cards.q: Between sunset and sunrise, an aircraft may not be operated unless it has
cards.why: Position lights are required from sunset to sunrise. Anticollision lights are required too if the aircraft has them.

cards.q: An aircraft's annual inspection is valid for
cards.why: An annual inspection is required within the preceding 12 calendar months.

cards.q: A 100-hour inspection is required for an aircraft that is
c: used to carry passengers for hire or used by a flight instructor who provides the aircraft for flight training
privately owned and flown more than 100 hours a year
cards.why: 100-hour inspections apply to aircraft carrying people for hire, or furnished by the person giving flight instruction for hire.

cards.q: The 100-hour inspection limit may be exceeded by not more than
c: 10 hours, to reach a place where the inspection can be done
cards.why: Up to 10 hours, only to reach a place where it can be done. The excess counts toward the next 100 hours.

cards.q: A transponder must have been tested and inspected within the preceding
cards.why: Transponders need a test and inspection every 24 calendar months.

cards.q: An emergency locator transmitter battery must be replaced (or recharged, if rechargeable) after
c: 1 cumulative hour of use or 50 percent of its useful life
cards.why: Replace or recharge it after 1 cumulative hour of use, or when 50 percent of its useful life (or charge) has expired.

cards.q: Who is primarily responsible for keeping an aircraft in an airworthy condition?
c: The mechanic who signed the last annual
The pilot who last flew it
cards.why: The owner or operator is primarily responsible for maintaining the aircraft in an airworthy condition, including complying with ADs.

cards.q: Airworthiness Directives are
c: mandatory corrections for unsafe conditions on aircraft, engines, propellers or appliances
voluntary service bulletins from the manufacturer
only for aircraft used for hire
cards.why: ADs are regulatory and mandatory (14 CFR Part 39). Compliance must be recorded in the maintenance records.

cards.q: The airworthiness certificate must be displayed
c: at the cabin or cockpit entrance, legible to passengers or crew
in the glove box with the registration
cards.why: It must be displayed at the cabin or flight deck entrance so it is legible to passengers or crew.

cards.q: Which instrument or equipment is required for day VFR flight in a powered airplane?
c: An airspeed indicator, altimeter and magnetic direction indicator
An attitude indicator and heading indicator
A turn coordinator and vertical speed indicator
cards.why: Day VFR (ATOMATOFLAMES): Airspeed, Tachometer, Oil pressure, Manifold pressure (altitude engines), Altimeter, Temperature gauges, Oil temperature, Fuel gauge, Landing gear position, Anticollision lights (if certificated after March 11, 1996), Magnetic compass, ELT, Safety belts.

cards.q: For night VFR, in addition to the day VFR equipment, an airplane needs (FLAPS)
c: fuses, landing light (if for hire), anticollision lights, position lights and a source of electrical power
an attitude indicator, heading indicator and turn coordinator
a second radio and a transponder
cards.why: FLAPS: Fuses (spares), Landing light if operated for hire, Anticollision lights, Position lights, Source of electricity.

cards.q: Flight crew must use supplemental oxygen for the whole time they are above
cards.why: Above 12,500 to 14,000 ft MSL: crew uses oxygen for any time beyond 30 minutes. Above 14,000: crew at all times. Above 15,000: each occupant must be provided oxygen.

cards.q: Between 12,500 ft and 14,000 ft MSL, the required flight crew must use oxygen
c: for any part of the flight longer than 30 minutes at those altitudes
cards.why: Cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 ft up to 14,000 ft: oxygen after 30 minutes.

cards.q: Above what altitude must each occupant of the aircraft be provided with supplemental oxygen?
cards.why: Above 15,000 ft MSL cabin pressure altitude, every occupant must be provided oxygen (they need not use it).

cards.q: Unless otherwise authorized, an operable transponder with altitude reporting is required
c: within 30 NM of a Class B primary airport, from the surface up to 10,000 ft MSL
cards.why: The Mode C veil: within 30 NM of the primary airport of Class B, from the surface to 10,000 ft MSL. Also in Class A, B and C and above 10,000 ft MSL (excluding at or below 2,500 ft AGL).

cards.q: Above what altitude is a Mode C transponder (and ADS-B Out) required in the contiguous US, excluding airspace at and below 2,500 ft AGL?
cards.why: Above 10,000 ft MSL, except at and below 2,500 ft AGL.

cards.q: Before entering Class D airspace, a pilot must
c: establish two-way radio communication with the control tower
receive an explicit clearance to enter
cards.why: Class D requires two-way radio communication before entering. If the controller responds with your call sign, communication is established.

cards.q: You call approach control before entering Class C airspace and hear: "Aircraft calling Charlotte Approach, standby." May you enter?
c: No. Your call sign wasn't used, so two-way communication isn't established
Yes. Any reply from the controller is enough
Yes, if you have a Mode C transponder
cards.why: Two-way radio communication requires the controller to respond using your call sign.

cards.q: To enter Class B airspace, a VFR pilot needs
cards.why: Class B needs a clearance, plus a private certificate (or a student endorsement), a Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out.

cards.q: Which equipment is required to operate in Class C airspace?
c: A two-way radio, a Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out
A VOR receiver and a transponder
cards.why: Class C: two-way radio, Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out.

cards.q: Which airspace has a floor of 18,000 ft MSL and requires IFR?
cards.why: Class A is 18,000 ft MSL up to and including FL600. All operations must be IFR.

cards.q: Unless designated lower, Class E airspace begins at
cards.why: Class E generally starts at 1,200 ft AGL unless charted lower (700 ft AGL with a magenta vignette, or at the surface).

cards.q: The vertical limit of Class C airspace is normally
cards.why: Class C: surface area of 5 NM radius up to 4,000 ft above the airport, and a shelf from 5 to 10 NM, 1,200 to 4,000 ft above the airport.
