cards.q: Class D airspace normally extends from the surface up to
cards.why: Class D normally extends to 2,500 ft above the airport, charted in MSL, and is drawn with a dashed blue line.

cards.q: When the control tower at a Class D airport closes, the airspace normally becomes
c: Class E or Class G, as shown in the Chart Supplement
cards.why: Without the tower, the surface area reverts to Class E (if weather reporting is available) or Class G.

cards.q: In a prohibited area, flight is
c: not allowed without permission of the using agency, which is rarely given
allowed with a clearance from ATC
cards.why: Prohibited areas (such as P-56 over the White House) are closed to flight for national security.

cards.q: Flying through a restricted area that is active requires
cards.why: Restricted areas contain unusual, often invisible hazards like artillery firing. When active, you need authorization from the controlling agency.

cards.q: VFR flight through an active Military Operations Area (MOA) is
c: permitted, but pilots should use extreme caution and contact the controlling agency for traffic advisories
permitted only with an ATC clearance
cards.why: MOAs separate military training from IFR traffic. VFR pilots may enter but should be vigilant.

cards.q: A warning area is airspace
c: extending from 3 NM outward from the US coast, containing activity that may be hazardous
over national parks where low flight is discouraged
cards.why: Warning areas lie over domestic or international waters beyond 3 NM from the coast.

cards.q: On the ground, FAA-designated Wildlife Refuges and National Parks ask pilots to keep a minimum altitude of
cards.why: Pilots are requested to stay at least 2,000 ft AGL over noise-sensitive areas such as national parks and wildlife refuges.

cards.q: How are temporary flight restrictions (TFRs) issued?
cards.why: TFRs are issued by NOTAM and can pop up with little notice. Check them before every flight.

cards.q: After an accident, the operator must file the NTSB written report within
cards.why: 10 days after an accident, or 7 days after an overdue aircraft is still missing.

cards.q: Which incident requires immediate notification to the NTSB?
c: A bird strike with no damage
cards.why: 830.5 lists incidents such as flight control system failure, in-flight fire, collision in flight and crewmember inability to perform duties.

cards.q: Wreckage from an aircraft accident may be moved before the NTSB takes custody
c: only to protect the wreckage from further damage, or to remove people or protect the public
to clear a runway, after 24 hours
cards.why: Preserve wreckage, cargo and records. Disturb them only to remove injured people, protect the wreckage, or protect the public.

cards.q: When the FAA receives a NASA Aviation Safety Reporting System (ASRS) report filed within 10 days of an inadvertent violation
c: no civil penalty or certificate suspension is imposed, if the conditions are met
the pilot is automatically cleared of any wrongdoing
the report is forwarded to the FAA for enforcement
cards.why: If the violation was inadvertent, not criminal, not an accident, and you file within 10 days, sanctions are waived (you may still be found in violation).

cards.q: Which preflight action is required before flying a cross-country flight with a passenger in a rented airplane?
c: Check weather, fuel requirements, alternatives and known traffic delays
File a flight plan with Flight Service
Get a briefing from the airplane's owner
cards.why: Preflight action under 91.103 covers all available information, including weather, fuel, alternatives and delays.

cards.q: An ATC clearance has been received. A pilot may deviate from it
c: in an emergency, or to respond to a TCAS resolution advisory, notifying ATC as soon as possible
whenever the pilot feels it is safer
only after filing a written request
cards.why: You may deviate only in an emergency (or for a TCAS RA) unless an amended clearance is obtained, and must notify ATC.

cards.q: If ATC gives you priority in an emergency, you may be asked to submit a detailed report within
cards.why: A pilot given priority in an emergency submits a report within 48 hours to the ATC facility manager, if requested.

cards.q: Unless the airport has a control tower, the traffic pattern direction you must use is
c: left turns, unless the airport shows otherwise with light signals or visual markings
the direction the first aircraft in the pattern chose
right turns at airports with more than one runway
cards.why: At airports without an operating tower, make all turns to the left unless markings or light signals show right turns.

cards.q: The standard (average) temperature lapse rate in the lower atmosphere is about
cards.why: The standard lapse rate is about 2°C per 1,000 ft. Dry rising air cools faster, about 3°C per 1,000 ft (the dry adiabatic rate).

cards.q: Standard sea-level conditions are
cards.why: The International Standard Atmosphere at sea level: 15°C (59°F) and 29.92 inHg (1013.2 hPa).

cards.q: Surface temperature 20°C, dew point 9°C. About how high are the bases of cumuliform clouds?
cards.why: Divide the temperature/dew point spread by 2.5°C (or 4.4°F) per 1,000 ft: 11 ÷ 2.5 ≈ 4.4, so about 4,400 ft AGL.

cards.q: Surface temperature 72°F and dew point 50°F. Estimate the base of convective clouds.
cards.why: A 22°F spread ÷ 4.4°F per 1,000 ft = 5,000 ft AGL.

cards.q: The dew point is
c: the temperature to which air must be cooled to become saturated
the temperature at which dew can no longer form
the lowest temperature reached at night
cards.why: Cool air to its dew point and it's saturated: clouds, fog or dew form. A small spread means fog or low clouds are likely.

cards.q: What happens to the amount of water vapor air can hold as its temperature rises?
cards.why: Warm air can hold more water vapor than cold air.

cards.q: Which characteristics describe an unstable air mass?
c: Cumuliform clouds, turbulence, good visibility outside showers, showery precipitation
Stratiform clouds, smooth air, poor visibility, continuous precipitation
Fog and low stratus with calm winds
cards.why: Unstable air rises on its own: towering clouds, bumpy air and showers, with good visibility between them.

cards.q: A temperature inversion is a layer in which
cards.why: In an inversion it gets warmer with height. The air below is very stable, so expect smooth air, haze, smoke and poor visibility.

cards.q: A common type of ground-based temperature inversion forms
c: on clear, cool nights with calm or light winds
cards.why: On clear calm nights the ground radiates heat away and cools the air next to it, making a surface inversion.

cards.q: Which stage of a thunderstorm is marked mainly by continuous updrafts?
cards.why: Cumulus stage: updrafts build the cloud. Mature: precipitation reaches the surface and up- and downdrafts both exist. Dissipating: downdrafts dominate.

cards.q: The beginning of the mature stage of a thunderstorm is signaled by
c: precipitation beginning to fall from the cloud base
the appearance of an anvil top
a sudden wind shift at the surface hours before the storm
cards.why: When rain or hail starts falling out of the base, downdrafts have begun: the storm is mature and at its most intense.

cards.q: Which thunderstorms generally produce the most intense hazards, such as hail, tornadoes and severe turbulence?
cards.why: A squall line is a non-frontal band of active thunderstorms, often ahead of a cold front, with the most severe weather.

cards.q: You should avoid a severe thunderstorm by at least
cards.why: Turbulence and hail can extend well outside the cloud. Give severe storms at least 20 NM, and don't fly under the anvil.

cards.q: Lightning is always associated with
cards.why: All thunderstorms produce lightning and have the potential for severe turbulence.

cards.q: Which type of fog forms on clear nights with light or calm winds over low, flat land?
cards.why: Radiation fog forms when the ground cools the air to its dew point on still, clear nights. It usually burns off after sunrise.

cards.q: Upslope fog forms when
c: moist, stable air is forced up sloping terrain and cooled
cold air moves over warm water
cards.why: Air pushed up a slope cools adiabatically to its dew point. Common along the eastern slopes of the Rockies.

cards.q: Steam fog forms when
c: cold, dry air moves over warmer water
warm, moist air moves over cold water
rain falls through cold air near the surface
cards.why: Evaporation from the warm water saturates the cold air above it. Steam fog is often associated with low-level turbulence and icing.

cards.q: Frost forms on an aircraft when
c: the collecting surface is at or below the dew point of the adjacent air, and the dew point is below freezing
small drops of rain freeze on contact
the air temperature is below freezing and there is fog
cards.why: Frost is water vapor depositing directly as ice. Remove all of it before flight: it disrupts airflow, reduces lift and raises stall speed.

cards.q: How does frost on the wings affect an airplane?
c: It spoils the smooth airflow, decreasing lift and increasing drag and stall speed
It adds weight but doesn't change lift
It has no effect if the frost is thin
cards.why: Even a thin, rough layer of frost can prevent takeoff by reducing lift and raising stall speed.

cards.q: For structural icing to form, there must be
c: visible moisture and an airframe temperature at or below freezing
high humidity and temperatures between 20°F and 70°F
cards.why: Structural ice needs visible moisture (cloud, rain, drizzle) and a surface at or below 0°C.

cards.q: Encountering freezing rain at your altitude is evidence that
c: there is warmer air (above freezing) at a higher altitude
a cold front has just passed
the air above you is colder
cards.why: Rain forms in warmer air aloft and falls into a subfreezing layer. Climbing into the warm layer, or turning back, is the way out.

cards.q: When a cold front passes, you typically see
c: a drop in temperature, a wind shift and rising pressure
a rise in temperature and falling pressure
steady rain and decreasing visibility for days
cards.why: Behind a cold front: colder, often clearer air, winds shift (usually to the northwest in the US) and pressure rises.

cards.q: One of the most easily recognized discontinuities across a front is
cards.why: Fronts separate air masses of different temperature. Wind direction and pressure changes also occur.

cards.q: Weather ahead of a warm front typically includes
c: stratiform clouds, steady precipitation and poor visibility, possibly fog
towering cumulus and showers with good visibility
cards.why: Warm air rides gently up over the cold air, giving widespread layered clouds and steady rain ahead of the front.

cards.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, air flows around a low-pressure area
cards.why: Around lows the wind flows counterclockwise and converges, rising and often producing clouds. Around highs it flows clockwise and outward.

cards.q: Why does the wind near the surface blow at an angle to the isobars, instead of parallel to them as it does aloft?
c: Surface friction slows the wind and reduces the Coriolis force
The pressure gradient is stronger near the surface
Temperature differences are larger near the ground
cards.why: Friction slows surface winds, so Coriolis force is weaker and the wind turns toward lower pressure.

cards.q: Wind shear can occur
c: at any altitude, in any direction
cards.why: Wind shear is a sudden change in wind speed or direction over a short distance. It's most dangerous close to the ground.

cards.q: Low-level wind shear is possible above a temperature inversion when
c: the winds just above the inversion are 25 knots or more
the surface winds are calm and the sky is overcast
cards.why: A strong wind just above a calm, inverted surface layer can cause a sudden airspeed change as you climb or descend through it.

cards.q: A microburst's downdraft can be as strong as
cards.why: Microbursts are small (about 1 km or less), short-lived (2 to 4 minutes at peak) downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm, with horizontal winds up to 45 knots.

cards.q: Flying into a microburst on approach, you would first expect
c: an increasing headwind and a performance increase
a downdraft before any change in airspeed
cards.why: First a headwind (airspeed up, the airplane balloons), then the downdraft, then a tailwind that can leave you low and slow.

cards.q: Mountain wave turbulence is likely when
c: strong winds of 25 knots or more blow across a ridge in stable air
winds are light and the air is unstable
a warm front approaches the mountains
cards.why: Stable air flowing over mountains forms standing waves. Look for lenticular and rotor clouds, but waves can exist without them.

cards.q: Clouds are classified into four families. Which is one of them?
cards.why: Low, middle, high, and clouds with vertical development (cumulus and cumulonimbus).

cards.q: The suffix "nimbus" in a cloud name means
c: a cloud with a flat base
cards.why: Nimbus means rain-bearing, as in nimbostratus and cumulonimbus. Alto means middle; cirro means high.

cards.q: Which cloud type would most likely produce severe turbulence and hail?
cards.why: Cumulonimbus is the thunderstorm cloud: severe turbulence, hail, icing, lightning and wind shear.

cards.q: In a METAR, the wind group 27015G25KT means
c: wind from 270° true at 15 knots, gusting to 25 knots
wind from 270° magnetic at 15 knots, gusting to 25 knots
wind from 270° true at 25 knots, gusting to 15 knots
cards.why: METAR winds are true direction and knots. Winds given by ATIS or a tower are magnetic.

cards.q: In a METAR, "BKN008 OVC015" means the ceiling is
cards.why: The ceiling is the lowest broken or overcast layer (or vertical visibility). Heights are hundreds of feet above ground level.

cards.q: What does "+TSRA" mean in a METAR?
cards.why: + is heavy, - is light, no sign is moderate. TS is thunderstorm, RA is rain.

cards.q: In a METAR, "VV005" means
c: an indefinite ceiling with vertical visibility of 500 ft
cards.why: VV is vertical visibility into an obscuration, such as fog. It counts as a ceiling.

cards.q: The remark "RMK AO2" in a METAR means
c: an automated station with a precipitation discriminator
cards.why: AO1: automated without a precipitation discriminator. AO2: automated with one (it can tell rain from snow).

cards.q: In a METAR, "A2992" means
cards.why: The A group is the altimeter setting in inches of mercury.

cards.q: A METAR shows "M04/M07". What are the temperature and dew point?
cards.why: M means minus. METAR temperatures are in degrees Celsius.

cards.q: How often are routine METARs issued?
cards.why: METARs are hourly. A SPECI is a special report issued when conditions change significantly.

cards.q: In a TAF, "FM1600" means
c: a rapid change in conditions starting at 1600Z
temporary conditions lasting less than an hour after 1600Z
cards.why: FM (from) starts a new forecast period with a significant change at that time.

cards.q: In a TAF, "TEMPO 1520/1523 1SM BR" means
c: temporary fluctuations to 1 SM in mist, each lasting less than an hour, between 2000Z and 2300Z on the 15th
a permanent change to 1 SM in mist at 2000Z
cards.why: TEMPO is temporary fluctuations of less than an hour, covering less than half the period.

cards.q: In a TAF, "PROB30" means
c: a 30 percent probability of the conditions during the period
cards.why: PROB30 or PROB40 gives the probability of thunderstorms or precipitation in that period.

cards.q: In a TAF, "SKC" or "P6SM" means
c: sky clear and visibility greater than 6 statute miles
cards.why: P6SM means plus 6 statute miles: visibility greater than 6 SM.

cards.q: AIRMET Sierra describes
c: IFR conditions and extensive mountain obscuration
moderate turbulence and strong surface winds
cards.why: Sierra: IFR and mountain obscuration. Tango: turbulence, sustained surface winds of 30 kt or more, low-level wind shear. Zulu: icing and freezing levels.

cards.q: Which AIRMET advises of moderate turbulence and sustained surface winds of 30 knots or more?
cards.why: Tango covers turbulence, strong surface winds and nonconvective low-level wind shear.

cards.q: AIRMET Zulu advises of
cards.why: Zulu is icing (and freezing-level heights).

cards.q: A convective SIGMET is issued for
c: tornadoes, lines of thunderstorms, embedded thunderstorms, large hail or severe surface winds
cards.why: Convective SIGMETs cover severe convective weather, including hail ≥ 3/4 inch and surface winds ≥ 50 kt. Any convective SIGMET implies severe turbulence, icing and wind shear.

cards.q: What is the purpose of a pilot weather report (PIREP)?
c: To report actual weather observed in flight, such as turbulence, icing, cloud tops and bases
To forecast weather along a route
To file a VFR flight plan
cards.why: PIREPs give real conditions aloft. UA is routine; UUA is urgent (severe turbulence, severe icing, wind shear, hail, volcanic ash).

cards.q: On a winds and temperatures aloft forecast (FB), wind direction is given relative to
c: true north, with speed in knots
magnetic north, with speed in knots
true north, with speed in miles per hour
cards.why: Forecast winds aloft are true direction in knots, and temperatures in Celsius.

cards.q: Decode the winds aloft group "7325-07".
cards.why: A direction code above 36 means speed is 100 knots or more: subtract 50 from the direction (73 − 50 = 23, so 230°) and add 100 to the speed (25 + 100 = 125 kt).

cards.q: On a winds aloft forecast, "9900" means
c: light and variable winds (less than 5 knots)
cards.why: 9900 means light and variable, under 5 knots.

cards.q: Why is there no wind forecast for the 3,000 ft level at a station 2,000 ft above sea level?
c: Winds aren't forecast within 1,500 ft of the station elevation
The station doesn't measure winds below 6,000 ft
Surface friction makes the forecast useless at all stations
cards.why: No winds within 1,500 ft of station elevation, and no temperatures for the 3,000 ft level or within 2,500 ft of station elevation.

cards.q: A surface analysis chart shows
c: actual positions of fronts, pressure systems and observed weather at the chart time
areas of forecast turbulence and icing
cards.why: The surface analysis is an observation: fronts, highs and lows, isobars and station models, updated every 3 hours.

cards.q: Closely spaced isobars on a surface analysis chart indicate
cards.why: The closer the isobars, the steeper the pressure gradient and the stronger the wind.

cards.q: Prognostic (prog) charts show
c: forecast positions of fronts and pressure systems and expected weather
observed weather at the time of the chart
cards.why: Progs are forecasts, issued for several times such as 12, 24, 48 and 72 hours ahead.

cards.q: Which source gives the most complete preflight weather picture, recorded for your flight?
c: A standard briefing from Flight Service (or an equivalent online briefing)
The ATIS at your departure airport
cards.why: Request a standard briefing if you haven't had one. An abbreviated briefing fills in gaps; an outlook briefing is for flights 6 or more hours away.

cards.q: You plan to depart in 8 hours. Which briefing should you request?
cards.why: Outlook briefings are for departures 6 or more hours away. Get a standard briefing closer to the time.

cards.q: The Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA) tool shows
c: observations and forecasts of clouds, weather, winds, icing and turbulence for the contiguous US
only TAFs and METARs in text form
cards.why: The GFA (aviationweather.gov) replaced the area forecast for the contiguous US.

cards.q: Weather radar on a ground-based radar display mainly shows
cards.why: Radar sees precipitation, not clouds or turbulence. Heavy precipitation often means strong convection.

cards.q: What does a dew point spread that is narrowing late in the evening suggest?
c: Fog or low clouds may form
cards.why: When the spread drops to a few degrees, saturation is close. Fog often forms overnight.

cards.q: Convective circulation patterns associated with sea breezes are caused by
c: cool, dense air over the water moving inland to replace warm air rising over the land
warm air over the water moving inland
pressure differences between two weather systems
cards.why: Land heats faster during the day; air rises there and cooler sea air flows in. At night the flow reverses (land breeze).

cards.q: Turbulence is most likely when flying over
c: plowed fields and paved areas on a hot day
lakes and forests on a cool day
cards.why: Dark, dry surfaces heat quickly and create rising currents; water and vegetation create sinking or calmer air.

cards.q: If the temperature and dew point are close together and you are in an area of high humidity, which is most likely?
c: Carburetor ice, fog or low clouds
cards.why: Close temperature and dew point mean nearly saturated air. Watch for fog, low ceilings and carb ice.

cards.q: Hazardous weather information broadcasts (HIWAS) are
c: continuous recorded broadcasts of AIRMETs, SIGMETs and other hazards over selected VORs
live reports from pilots in flight
radar updates from a control tower
cards.why: HIWAS summaries are broadcast over selected VOR frequencies. Not all areas have them.

cards.q: Where can you get updates on weather in flight from a Flight Service specialist?
c: On the published Flight Service frequency, such as 122.2 MHz, or a remote communications outlet
cards.why: Flight Service specialists are reachable on published FSS frequencies (122.2 is common) and RCOs.

cards.q: One degree of latitude equals about
cards.why: 1° of latitude is 60 NM, and 1 minute of latitude is 1 NM. Use the latitude scale on a meridian to measure distance.

cards.q: Lines of longitude (meridians) run
c: from pole to pole, measuring east and west of the prime meridian
parallel to the equator, measuring north and south
cards.why: Meridians run north–south and measure longitude east or west of Greenwich. Parallels of latitude run east–west.

cards.q: On a sectional chart, a true course should be measured
c: at the meridian nearest the midpoint of the course
cards.why: Meridians converge toward the poles, so measure the course angle near the middle of the route.

cards.q: True course 105°, variation 10°E. What is the magnetic course?
cards.why: "East is least, west is best": subtract easterly variation, add westerly. 105 − 10 = 095.

cards.q: True course 230°, variation 8°W. What is the magnetic course?
cards.why: Add westerly variation: 230 + 8 = 238.

cards.q: Magnetic variation is
c: the angle between true north and magnetic north
the error in a compass caused by the airplane's electrical equipment
the difference between heading and course
cards.why: Variation changes with location and is shown by isogonic lines on charts. Deviation is the compass error caused by the airplane itself.

cards.q: Compass deviation is caused by
c: magnetic fields within the airplane, such as metal parts and electrical equipment
the difference between true and magnetic north
cards.why: Deviation varies with heading and is shown on a compass correction card in the airplane.

cards.q: Isogonic lines on a sectional chart connect points of
cards.why: Isogonic lines are dashed magenta lines labeled with the variation, such as 5°E. The agonic line has zero variation.

cards.q: The order of course and heading corrections from a true course to a compass heading is
c: true course, wind correction, variation, deviation
true course, deviation, variation, wind correction
cards.why: TC ± WCA = TH; TH ± variation = MH; MH ± deviation = CH. ("True virgins make dull company".)

cards.q: Flying a true course of 090° with a wind from the north, you'll need to
c: turn left of course (into the wind) to correct for drift
keep the heading equal to the course
cards.why: Crab into the wind. A north wind pushes you south (right of an eastbound course), so head left of 090.

cards.q: How far will you fly in 20 minutes at a groundspeed of 105 knots?
How long will it take to fly 84 NM at a groundspeed of 112 knots?
Your airplane burns 9.5 gallons per hour. How much fuel will a 1 hour 20 minute flight use?
cards.why: 9.5 × 1.333 h ≈ 12.7 gallons, before adding the required reserve.

cards.q: You have 40 gallons usable, burn 10 gph and must keep a 30-minute day VFR reserve. What is the maximum flight time?
cards.why: 40 gallons ÷ 10 gph = 4.0 h total; minus 0.5 h reserve = 3.5 hours.

cards.q: Two checkpoints 15 NM apart take 10 minutes to fly between. What is your groundspeed?
cards.why: 15 NM in 1/6 hour = 90 knots.

cards.q: Using the 1-in-60 rule, you are 2 NM off course after flying 30 NM. How far is your track off course?
cards.why: Each NM off course after 60 NM is 1°. 2 NM off after 30 NM = 2 × (60 ÷ 30) = 4°.

cards.q: Pilotage is navigation by
c: computing heading and time from known wind
cards.why: Pilotage uses landmarks. Dead reckoning uses computed headings, groundspeeds and times. Most VFR flights use both.

cards.q: Dead reckoning is navigation based on
c: computations of time, speed, distance and direction
cards.why: Dead reckoning predicts your position from heading, true airspeed, wind and elapsed time.

cards.q: If you become lost, the recommended actions are the four Cs. Which list matches them?
cards.why: Climb for better visibility and radio range, communicate (121.5 or Flight Service), confess you're lost, comply with instructions. Also conserve fuel.

cards.q: A VOR radial is
c: a magnetic bearing extending outward from the VOR station
a true bearing toward the station
a course defined by two VORs
cards.why: Radials are FROM the station, referenced to magnetic north. Flying inbound on the 090 radial means a course of 270.

cards.q: You want to fly directly to a VOR. The OBS is set so the CDI centers with a TO flag. Your course to the station is
c: the course shown under the OBS index
the reciprocal of the course shown
the radial shown under the OBS index
cards.why: With a TO flag and a centered needle, the OBS course takes you to the station.

cards.q: Inbound to a VOR on the 240 radial, what course should you set in the OBS?
cards.why: Inbound on the 240 radial, you fly the reciprocal: 060°, with a TO flag.

cards.q: The CDI needle on a VOR is deflected fully to one side. How far off the selected course are you?
cards.why: Full-scale deflection is 10° or more. On the common five-dot display, each dot is 2°.

cards.q: What should you hear to identify a VOR?
cards.why: Always identify the station by its Morse code (sometimes also a voice ID). No identifier can mean the station is under maintenance and unreliable.

cards.q: Why might a VOR become unusable at low altitude far from the station?
cards.why: VHF signals travel in straight lines, so terrain and the earth's curvature block them at low altitude.

cards.q: What is the maximum allowable error for a VOR check using a VOT (VOR test signal)?
cards.why: VOT and ground checkpoint: ±4°. Airborne checkpoint: ±6°. Dual VOR check: within 4° of each other.

cards.q: When using a VOT, the CDI should center with the OBS set to 360° and a flag reading
cards.why: "Cessna 182": 180-TO, 360-FROM. With the OBS on 360°, the VOT check shows FROM.

cards.q: Before using GPS for navigation, you should check that
c: the database is current and the receiver has enough satellites (integrity monitoring available)
the VOR is tuned to the same station
cards.why: Use a current database and check RAIM (or WAAS integrity). Cross-check against charts.

cards.q: What does ADS-B Out do?
c: Broadcasts the aircraft's GPS position, altitude and other data to ATC and other aircraft
Displays weather and traffic in the cockpit
Replaces the need for a transponder everywhere
cards.why: ADS-B Out transmits; ADS-B In receives traffic (TIS-B) and weather (FIS-B). ADS-B Out is required where Mode C is required.

cards.q: On a sectional chart, an airport drawn in blue has
cards.why: Blue airport symbols are towered. Magenta are non-towered.

cards.q: On a sectional chart, Class B airspace is shown by
cards.why: Class B: solid blue. Class C: solid magenta. Class D: dashed blue. Class E surface area: dashed magenta.

cards.q: On a sectional chart, a dashed magenta line around an airport shows
c: Class E airspace beginning at the surface
Class E airspace beginning at 700 ft AGL
cards.why: A dashed magenta line is a Class E surface area. A faded magenta vignette shows Class E starting at 700 ft AGL.

cards.q: On a sectional chart, a magenta vignette (shaded band) around an airport shows
c: Class E airspace begins at 700 ft AGL inside the shaded area
Class G airspace extends to 14,500 ft
cards.why: Inside the magenta vignette Class E starts at 700 ft AGL. A blue vignette marks where Class E starts at 1,200 ft AGL.

cards.q: On a sectional chart, "[45]" inside Class D airspace means
c: the ceiling of the Class D airspace is 4,500 ft MSL
the floor of Class D is 4,500 ft
cards.why: A number in a box (square brackets) inside Class D shows its ceiling in hundreds of feet MSL.

cards.q: In Class B or C airspace on a sectional, "70/30" in a sector means
c: the airspace extends from 3,000 ft MSL to 7,000 ft MSL
the airspace extends from 7,000 ft to 30,000 ft
the speed limit is 70 knots below 3,000 ft
cards.why: Ceiling over floor, in hundreds of feet MSL.

cards.q: On a sectional chart, an obstruction shown as "1532 (512)" has
c: a top at 1,532 ft MSL, 512 ft above the ground
a top at 512 ft MSL, 1,532 ft above the ground
cards.why: The bold number is the top in feet MSL; the number in parentheses is its height AGL.

cards.q: The maximum elevation figure (MEF) in each quadrangle of a sectional chart shows
c: the highest elevation of terrain or obstacles in that quadrangle, rounded up, in thousands and hundreds of feet MSL
the minimum safe altitude for IFR flight
the highest airport elevation in the area
cards.why: The large blue number (such as 3⁵ = 3,500 ft MSL) covers the highest terrain or obstruction, plus a buffer.

cards.q: On a sectional chart, a military training route labeled "IR 1206" is flown
c: under IFR, at or below 1,500 ft AGL
cards.why: IR is IFR, VR is VFR. Four-digit numbers: at or below 1,500 ft AGL. Three digits: some segments above 1,500 ft AGL. Military jets can fly them over 250 knots.

cards.q: The airport data "122.8 C" on a sectional chart shows
c: a CTAF (common traffic advisory frequency) of 122.8
cards.why: A C in a solid circle marks the CTAF. A star after the frequency means it's part-time.

cards.q: Where would you find an airport's pattern altitude, fuel available and runway details?
cards.why: The Chart Supplement (formerly the Airport/Facility Directory) lists airport details, frequencies and remarks.

cards.q: Before flying near a Class B or C airport, which chart gives the most detail about its airspace and VFR checkpoints?
cards.why: Terminal area charts are 1:250,000 scale (twice the detail of a sectional) for Class B areas.

cards.q: Sectional charts are drawn at a scale of
cards.why: Sectionals are 1:500,000; terminal area charts are 1:250,000.

cards.q: An airplane's true airspeed is 110 knots and the wind is a direct headwind of 20 knots. What is the groundspeed?
cards.why: A direct headwind subtracts from true airspeed: 110 − 20 = 90 knots.

cards.q: A VFR flight plan is
c: optional, but it starts search and rescue if you don't arrive and close it
cards.why: VFR flight plans are filed with Flight Service. If not closed within 30 minutes after your ETA, search procedures begin.

cards.q: If you don't close your VFR flight plan, search and rescue procedures normally begin
c: 30 minutes after your estimated time of arrival
cards.why: Flight Service starts looking for you 30 minutes after your ETA. Close the plan as soon as you land.

cards.q: To receive VFR flight following (radar traffic advisories) en route, you
c: contact ATC and request it; it's provided on a workload-permitting basis
must file an IFR flight plan
cards.why: Flight following is a basic radar service for VFR aircraft, workload permitting.

cards.q: In straight-and-level, unaccelerated flight
c: lift equals weight and thrust equals drag
lift is greater than weight and thrust is greater than drag
cards.why: In steady flight the opposing forces balance: the sum of the upward forces equals the downward forces, and thrust equals drag.

cards.q: The angle of attack is the angle between
c: the wing's chord line and the relative wind
the longitudinal axis and the horizon
the chord line and the longitudinal axis
cards.why: The angle between chord line and relative wind. The angle of incidence is between the chord line and the longitudinal axis, and the pilot can't change it.

cards.q: The relative wind is
c: opposite and parallel to the airplane's flightpath
cards.why: Relative wind flows opposite to the direction the wing moves through the air.

cards.q: Bernoulli's principle states that as the velocity of a fluid increases, its pressure
cards.why: Faster-moving air over the curved upper surface has lower pressure, which contributes to lift.

cards.q: An airplane can stall
c: at any airspeed, in any attitude, at any power setting
only at low airspeed with the nose high
cards.why: A stall happens whenever the critical angle of attack is exceeded, regardless of airspeed, attitude or weight.

cards.q: If airspeed decreases in level flight, the angle of attack must
c: increase to maintain the same lift
decrease to maintain the same lift
cards.why: Lift depends on angle of attack and airspeed squared. Slower means a higher angle of attack, until the critical angle is reached.

cards.q: If airspeed is doubled, lift (at the same angle of attack) becomes
cards.why: Lift varies with the square of the velocity.

cards.q: Which drag increases as airspeed decreases?
cards.why: Induced drag is a byproduct of lift and is greatest at high angles of attack (low speed). Parasite drag grows with the square of airspeed.

cards.q: Total drag is lowest at the airspeed where
c: induced drag and parasite drag are equal
cards.why: That point is L/Dmax, which gives the best glide (and, for propeller airplanes, about the best range).

cards.q: Wingtip vortices are strongest when the generating airplane is
cards.why: Vortex strength depends on weight, speed and wing shape: heavy, clean (flaps up) and slow at a high angle of attack is worst.

cards.q: Ground effect is most noticeable when the airplane is
c: within about one-half of its wingspan above the ground
within about two wingspans above the ground
cards.why: Ground effect reduces induced drag and wingtip vortices within about one wingspan, and is significant below about half a span.

cards.q: What does ground effect do?
c: Reduces induced drag, so the airplane may float on landing or lift off below the recommended speed
Increases induced drag and makes the airplane sink
cards.why: Less induced drag in ground effect: the airplane floats on landing and may become airborne too early on takeoff, then settle when it climbs out of it.

cards.q: An airplane leaving ground effect after takeoff will
c: need a higher angle of attack for the same lift, with more induced drag
need less thrust to maintain airspeed
experience a decrease in stall speed
cards.why: Out of ground effect, induced drag increases and the airplane may settle if it lifted off too slowly.

cards.q: At a load factor of 2, the stall speed increases by about
cards.why: Stall speed grows with the square root of the load factor: √2 ≈ 1.41, so about 41% higher.

cards.q: An airplane stalls at 50 knots in level flight. About what is its stall speed in a level 60° bank turn?
Maneuvering speed (Va) is
c: the maximum speed at which full, abrupt control movement won't overstress the airplane
the speed for the best rate of climb
the maximum speed in turbulence for passenger comfort
cards.why: At or below Va, the airplane stalls before exceeding its limit load factor. Va decreases as weight decreases.

cards.q: As an airplane's weight decreases, maneuvering speed
cards.why: A lighter airplane reaches the critical angle of attack, and the limit load, at a lower speed.

cards.q: The limit load factor for a normal category airplane is
What causes an airplane (except a T-tail) to pitch nose down when power is reduced, with no trim change?
c: Less downwash on the horizontal stabilizer from the propeller slipstream
The center of gravity moves forward
Thrust acts below the center of gravity
cards.why: Slipstream over the tail produces a downward force; less power means less of it, so the nose pitches down.

cards.q: An airplane loaded with the CG forward of the forward limit will
c: have a higher stall speed and be harder to flare
cards.why: A forward CG needs more tail-down force: more effective weight, higher stall speed, and elevator authority may run out in the flare.

cards.q: An airplane loaded with the CG aft of the aft limit will
c: be less stable, with poor or impossible stall and spin recovery
be more stable and have a higher stall speed
cards.why: An aft CG reduces longitudinal stability and can make recovery from a stall or spin impossible.

cards.q: Longitudinal stability is about which axis?
cards.why: Stability in pitch is longitudinal stability, governed by the CG position relative to the center of lift and the horizontal tail.

cards.q: Positive static stability means that, after being displaced, an airplane
c: initially tends to return to its original attitude
continues moving away from its original attitude
cards.why: Static stability is the initial tendency. Dynamic stability describes what happens over time.

cards.q: Which of these is a left-turning tendency in a single-engine propeller airplane?
cards.why: Torque, P-factor (asymmetric propeller thrust), spiraling slipstream and gyroscopic precession all yaw a clockwise-turning (from the cockpit) propeller airplane left.

cards.q: P-factor causes the airplane to yaw left when it is at
c: high angles of attack with high power
cards.why: The descending right-side propeller blade has a higher angle of attack and makes more thrust than the ascending blade.

cards.q: Gyroscopic precession is most noticeable
c: when the tail of a tailwheel airplane is raised during the takeoff roll
cards.why: Pitching the spinning propeller disk down applies a force that acts 90° later in rotation, yawing the airplane left.

cards.q: Adverse yaw is caused by
c: more induced drag on the outside (raised) wing when the ailerons are deflected
cards.why: The wing whose aileron goes down makes more lift and more induced drag, yawing the nose away from the turn. Coordinate with rudder.

cards.q: In a skidding turn, the ball of the turn coordinator is
c: displaced toward the outside of the turn
displaced toward the inside of the turn
cards.why: In a skid the rate of turn is too great for the bank, so the ball goes to the outside. In a slip it goes to the inside. Step on the ball.

cards.q: Why is a skidding turn near the ground (for example, base to final) especially dangerous?
c: It can lead to a cross-controlled stall and an incipient spin with little altitude to recover
cards.why: Too much inside rudder with opposite aileron in a turn can stall the inside wing first and start a spin.

cards.q: For a spin to occur, the airplane must be
c: at a high airspeed with full power
in a steep bank above maneuvering speed
cards.why: A spin is an aggravated stall with autorotation: both wings stalled, one more deeply than the other, plus yaw.

cards.q: The standard spin recovery for most light airplanes (PARE) begins with
c: power to idle, ailerons neutral, full opposite rudder, then elevator forward
full power and full back elevator
ailerons against the spin, then rudder with the spin
cards.why: PARE: Power idle, Ailerons neutral, Rudder opposite the spin, Elevator forward to break the stall. Always follow the POH.

cards.q: Lowering the flaps
c: increases lift and drag, allowing a steeper approach and a lower stall speed
cards.why: Flaps raise the wing's maximum lift coefficient and add drag, so you can approach slower and steeper.

cards.q: Wing washout (twist) is designed so that
c: the wing root stalls before the tip, keeping aileron control during a stall
the tip stalls before the root
both parts stall at the same time
cards.why: The tip has a lower angle of incidence, so the root stalls first and the ailerons keep working.

cards.q: Why is a propeller blade twisted along its length?
c: Because each section moves at a different speed, the twist gives a more uniform angle of attack and thrust along the blade
cards.why: The tip travels much faster than the hub, so the blade angle decreases toward the tip.

cards.q: The term "angle of incidence" refers to the angle between
c: the wing chord line and the airplane's longitudinal axis
the wing chord line and the relative wind
the airplane's longitudinal axis and the horizon
cards.why: It's fixed by design, unlike the angle of attack.

cards.q: Best glide speed gives
c: the greatest distance per foot of altitude lost (L/Dmax)
the longest time in the air
cards.why: Best glide is at L/Dmax. Minimum sink is slower and gives the most time aloft but less distance.

cards.q: If you glide at a speed slower than best glide speed, the glide distance will be
cards.why: Any speed other than best glide, faster or slower, shortens the glide.

cards.q: A headwind during a power-off glide will
c: decrease the distance covered over the ground
cards.why: The glide ratio through the air is the same, but groundspeed is lower, so you cover less ground. Many pilots glide slightly faster into a strong headwind.

cards.q: Vx is the airspeed that gives
c: the greatest altitude gain in a given distance (best angle of climb)
the greatest altitude gain in a given time
cards.why: Use Vx to clear obstacles after takeoff, Vy for the best rate of climb.

cards.q: As altitude increases, Vx and Vy
c: converge until they meet at the airplane's absolute ceiling
cards.why: Vx (indicated) increases slightly and Vy decreases until they are equal at the absolute ceiling.

cards.q: The airspeed indicator's white arc shows
c: the flap operating range, from Vs0 to Vfe
the caution range for smooth air only
cards.why: White: flap operating range. Green: normal range (Vs1 to Vno). Yellow: caution, smooth air only (Vno to Vne). Red line: Vne.

cards.q: The lower limit of the green arc on the airspeed indicator is
c: Vs1, the stall speed in a specified configuration (usually clean)
Vs0, the stall speed in landing configuration
cards.why: Vs1 is the bottom of the green arc. Vs0 is the bottom of the white arc.

cards.q: The upper limit of the green arc on the airspeed indicator is
c: Vno, the maximum structural cruising speed
cards.why: Vno tops the green arc. Fly in the yellow arc only in smooth air.

cards.q: Which V-speed is not marked on the airspeed indicator?
cards.why: Va isn't color-coded because it varies with weight. Find it in the POH or on a placard.

cards.q: Frost, dirt or ice on the wing surfaces will
c: reduce lift and increase stall speed
cards.why: Contamination disrupts the smooth airflow, reducing the maximum lift and raising stall speed.

cards.q: In a steep turn, if you don't add back pressure, the airplane will
cards.why: Banking tilts the lift vector, so the vertical component is less than weight. Increase the angle of attack (and often power) to hold altitude.

cards.q: In a steep turn (more than about 30° of bank), the overbanking tendency means
c: the bank tends to keep steepening, so you may need slight opposite aileron to hold it
the airplane tends to roll back to wings level
the bank stays constant with the controls neutral
cards.why: In a steep bank the outer wing travels faster and makes more lift than the inner wing, so the bank tends to increase.

cards.q: Pressure altitude is the altitude shown on the altimeter when it is set to
cards.why: Pressure altitude is height above the standard datum plane (29.92 inHg). It's used in performance charts and in Class A.

cards.q: Density altitude is
c: pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature
cards.why: Density altitude is the altitude in the standard atmosphere that has the same air density. The airplane performs as if it were at that altitude.

cards.q: Field elevation 1,380 ft, altimeter setting 30.12 inHg. What is the pressure altitude?
Field elevation 5,250 ft, altimeter setting 29.70 inHg. What is the pressure altitude?
Pressure altitude 5,000 ft and OAT 30°C. Using the rule of thumb, what is the density altitude?
cards.why: Standard temperature at 5,000 ft is 15 − (2 × 5) = 5°C. DA ≈ PA + 120 × (OAT − ISA) = 5,000 + 120 × 25 = 8,000 ft.

cards.q: What is the standard temperature at a pressure altitude of 6,000 ft?
Which combination gives the highest density altitude?
c: High elevation, high temperature, high humidity
Low elevation, low temperature, low humidity
High elevation, low temperature, low humidity
cards.why: Hot, high and humid air is least dense, so it has the highest density altitude and the worst performance.

cards.q: How does high humidity affect density altitude?
cards.why: Water vapor is lighter than the dry air it displaces, so humid air is less dense.

cards.q: At a high density altitude, you should expect
c: a longer takeoff roll and a reduced rate of climb
a shorter takeoff roll and a better rate of climb
no change if you use the same indicated airspeeds
cards.why: Less dense air means less engine power, less propeller thrust and less lift, so a higher true airspeed is needed for the same indicated airspeed.

cards.q: At a high-elevation airport on a hot day, the indicated airspeed for liftoff and approach should be
c: the same as usual, but the true airspeed and groundspeed will be higher
cards.why: Fly the normal indicated airspeeds. Your true airspeed and groundspeed will be higher, so takeoff and landing distances are longer.

cards.q: A headwind of 10 percent of the takeoff airspeed will reduce the takeoff distance by about
cards.why: PHAK: a 10% headwind cuts takeoff distance about 19%; a 10% tailwind increases it about 21%.

cards.q: A tailwind of 10 percent of the takeoff airspeed will increase the takeoff distance by about
cards.why: Tailwinds hurt more than headwinds help: about 21% longer for a 10% tailwind.

cards.q: A 10 percent increase in takeoff weight increases the takeoff distance by at least
cards.why: About 5% higher takeoff speed, at least 9% less acceleration and at least 21% more distance.

cards.q: Which runway condition increases the takeoff distance?
c: Tall grass, soft ground or an upslope
cards.why: Rolling friction and gravity both slow acceleration on soft, grassy or uphill surfaces.

cards.q: The minimum speed for dynamic hydroplaning with tires inflated to 36 psi is about
cards.why: Hydroplaning speed ≈ 9 × √(tire pressure in psi) = 9 × 6 = 54 knots.

cards.q: The maximum demonstrated crosswind velocity in the POH is
c: the highest crosswind tested during certification, not a structural limit
a regulatory limit you may never exceed
cards.why: It isn't a limitation, but exceeding it means you're beyond what test pilots demonstrated.

cards.q: Runway 01 (010°), wind 040° at 20 knots. What is the crosswind component?
cards.why: Angle 30°. Crosswind = 20 × sin 30° = 10 knots. Headwind = 20 × cos 30° ≈ 17 knots.

cards.q: Runway 27, wind 330° at 15 knots. What is the crosswind component?
cards.why: Angle 60°. Crosswind = 15 × sin 60° ≈ 13 knots. Headwind = 15 × cos 60° = 7.5 knots.

cards.q: Runway 18, wind 180° at 12 knots. What is the crosswind component?
cards.why: The wind is straight down the runway: all headwind, no crosswind.

cards.q: Rule of thumb: with the wind 45° off the runway, the crosswind component is about
cards.why: sin 30° = 0.5, sin 45° ≈ 0.7, sin 60° ≈ 0.9. At 90° it's all crosswind.

cards.q: A 10:1 glide ratio from 6,000 ft above the ground covers about
cards.why: 6,000 ft × 10 = 60,000 ft, and 60,000 ÷ 6,076 ft per NM ≈ 10 NM (in still air).

cards.q: Moment equals
cards.why: Moment (lb-in) = weight (lb) × arm (in). CG = total moment ÷ total weight.

cards.q: A 120-lb passenger sits at an arm of 85 inches. What is the moment?
The datum used for weight and balance is
c: an imaginary vertical plane, chosen by the manufacturer, from which all arms are measured
always the nose of the airplane
cards.why: The datum may be at the firewall, the nose or even ahead of the airplane. Arms aft of it are positive.

cards.q: Aviation gasoline (avgas) weighs about
cards.why: Avgas 6 lb/gal, oil 7.5 lb/gal, water 8.35 lb/gal, jet fuel about 6.7 lb/gal.

cards.q: How much do 38 gallons of avgas weigh?
cards.why: 38 × 6 = 228 pounds.

cards.q: Engine oil weighs about 7.5 pounds per gallon. How much do 8 quarts weigh?
cards.why: 8 quarts = 2 gallons; 2 × 7.5 = 15 pounds.

cards.q: Basic empty weight includes
c: the standard empty weight plus optional equipment, unusable fuel and full engine oil
the airplane, pilot and full fuel
cards.why: Basic empty weight = standard empty weight + optional equipment. It includes unusable fuel and full operating fluids, including full oil.

cards.q: Useful load is
c: the maximum gross weight minus the basic empty weight
the weight of the passengers and baggage only
the weight of the usable fuel
cards.why: Useful load = pilot, passengers, baggage and usable fuel. Payload is the part that isn't fuel or crew.

cards.q: Maximum gross weight 2,400 lb, basic empty weight 1,610 lb. What is the useful load?
cards.why: 2,400 − 1,610 = 790 lb, shared between people, baggage and usable fuel.

cards.q: Given: empty weight 1,500 lb at arm 38 in; front seats 340 lb at 37 in; rear seat 180 lb at 73 in; fuel 240 lb at 48 in; baggage 50 lb at 95 in. What is the CG?
Using the loading in the previous problem (total 2,310 lb), the maximum gross weight is 2,300 lb. What should you do?
c: Remove at least 10 lb, for example fuel or baggage, and recompute the CG
Nothing; 10 lb over is within tolerance
Move the baggage forward to fix the weight
cards.why: Moving weight changes the CG, not the total weight. You must offload at least 10 lb.

cards.q: Total weight 2,400 lb, CG 45.0 in. How much baggage must move from a 120-in arm to a 40-in arm to move the CG to 44.0 in?
cards.why: Weight shifted ÷ total weight = CG change ÷ distance moved. W = 2,400 × 1.0 ÷ 80 = 30 lb.

cards.q: Total weight 2,000 lb, CG 40 in. A 100-lb passenger moves from an arm of 36 in to an arm of 76 in. What is the new CG?
cards.why: CG change = 100 × 40 ÷ 2,000 = 2 in aft, so 42 in.

cards.q: Fuel is stored at an arm aft of the airplane's loaded CG. As fuel burns, the CG
cards.why: Removing weight that is aft of the CG moves the CG forward. Check that the CG stays within limits for the whole flight.

cards.q: Adding weight aft of the current CG will
cards.why: The CG moves toward added weight and away from removed weight.

cards.q: Which is an effect of overloading an airplane?
c: Higher takeoff speed, longer takeoff run, reduced climb rate and higher stall speed
Lower stall speed and shorter takeoff
cards.why: Excess weight degrades nearly every aspect of performance and can overstress the structure.

cards.q: Why does the POH list a maximum ramp weight higher than the maximum takeoff weight?
c: It allows for fuel burned during engine start, taxi and run-up
It allows for passengers who board at the runway
It is the weight limit for landing
cards.why: Ramp weight includes start, taxi and run-up fuel that will be burned before takeoff.

cards.q: What happens to the landing distance at a high density altitude?
c: It increases, because the true airspeed and groundspeed at touchdown are higher
It decreases, because the air is thinner
It doesn't change if you use the normal indicated approach speed
cards.why: The same indicated airspeed is a higher true airspeed, so there is more energy to dissipate on the ground.

cards.q: Absolute ceiling is the altitude at which
c: the airplane can no longer climb
the airplane can climb at 100 fpm
cards.why: Absolute ceiling: zero rate of climb. Service ceiling: maximum rate of climb is 100 fpm.

cards.q: Service ceiling is the altitude at which
c: the best rate of climb is 100 fpm
the airplane can no longer climb
cards.why: Service ceiling: 100 fpm best rate of climb. Absolute ceiling: no climb at all.

cards.q: When using a takeoff performance chart, you should normally enter it with
c: pressure altitude and temperature, then correct for weight, wind and runway
cards.why: Charts are built on pressure altitude and temperature (which together give density altitude).

cards.q: Which instruments use the pitot-static system?
c: Airspeed indicator, altimeter and vertical speed indicator
Attitude indicator, heading indicator and turn coordinator
Airspeed indicator, attitude indicator and altimeter
cards.why: The ASI uses pitot and static pressure; the altimeter and VSI use static pressure only. The gyro instruments don't use the pitot-static system.

cards.q: If the pitot tube's ram air inlet and drain hole are both blocked, the airspeed indicator will
c: act like an altimeter, reading higher as you climb and lower as you descend
cards.why: Trapped pitot pressure stays constant while static pressure changes with altitude.

cards.q: If only the pitot tube's ram air inlet is blocked (the drain hole is open), the airspeed indicator will
cards.why: Pitot pressure leaks out through the drain hole until it equals static pressure, so the ASI reads zero.

cards.q: If the static ports become blocked while you are in level flight, the altimeter will
c: freeze at the altitude where the blockage occurred
cards.why: The altimeter freezes and the VSI reads zero. The ASI becomes unreliable: it reads low when climbing and high when descending.

cards.q: With a blocked static system, as you descend the airspeed indicator will read
cards.why: Trapped static pressure is lower than the real static pressure as you descend, so the ASI overreads.

cards.q: Using the alternate static source (cabin air) in an unpressurized airplane usually makes the altimeter and airspeed indicator read
cards.why: Cabin pressure is a little lower than outside static pressure. The VSI briefly shows a climb when you switch over.

cards.q: Indicated altitude is
c: the altitude read directly from the altimeter when set to the current altimeter setting
height above the standard datum plane
cards.why: Indicated altitude approximates true altitude (MSL) when the altimeter is set to the local setting. Absolute altitude is height above ground.

cards.q: True altitude is
c: the actual height above mean sea level
cards.why: True altitude is MSL. Obstacles and terrain on charts are shown in true altitude.

cards.q: Absolute altitude is
cards.why: Absolute altitude is height above ground level.

cards.q: You fly from an area of high pressure to an area of low pressure without resetting the altimeter. Your true altitude will be
cards.why: "High to low, look out below." Reset the altimeter to the local setting en route.

cards.q: When flying in air colder than standard, the altimeter shows an altitude
cards.why: Cold air is denser, so the pressure levels sit lower: you are lower than indicated. Hot to cold, look out below too.

cards.q: If the altimeter setting is changed from 29.92 to 30.12, the indicated altitude will
cards.why: Each 0.01 inHg is about 10 ft. Turning the setting up raises the indicated altitude.

cards.q: If no altimeter setting is available before departure, set the altimeter to
cards.why: Setting field elevation gives the best estimate of the local setting.

cards.q: The vertical speed indicator shows
c: a trend immediately and an accurate rate after about 6 to 9 seconds
cards.why: The VSI compares current static pressure with pressure in a calibrated leak. Its rate lags behind trend.

cards.q: Gyroscopic instruments work on which two principles?
c: Bernoulli's principle and Newton's third law
cards.why: The attitude and heading indicators use rigidity in space; the turn coordinator uses precession.

cards.q: In most light airplanes, the attitude and heading indicators are powered by
cards.why: Usually a vacuum (suction) pump drives the AI and HI, while the turn coordinator is electric, so one failure won't take out all the gyros.

cards.q: How often should the heading indicator be checked against the magnetic compass in flight?
c: About every 15 minutes, in straight-and-level unaccelerated flight
cards.why: Precession (friction) makes the HI drift. Realign it with the compass when the compass is steady.

cards.q: The turn coordinator shows
c: the rate of roll and the rate of turn
cards.why: Its canted gyro senses roll and yaw. Aligned with the index mark, you're in a standard-rate turn (3° per second).

cards.q: A standard-rate turn is
c: 3° per second, a 360° turn in 2 minutes
cards.why: Standard rate: 3° per second. Bank angle for it ≈ (TAS ÷ 10) + 7.

cards.q: When turning to the north in the Northern Hemisphere, the magnetic compass will
c: lag behind the turn, so roll out before the compass reaches north
lead the turn, so roll out after the compass reaches north
cards.why: Northerly turning error: UNOS, Undershoot North, Overshoot South.

cards.q: On an easterly or westerly heading, accelerating makes the magnetic compass show a turn toward the
cards.why: ANDS: Accelerate North, Decelerate South.

cards.q: Magnetic compass errors from turning and acceleration are caused mainly by
cards.why: The compass card tilts toward the earth's magnetic field lines (dip), which causes turning and acceleration errors.

cards.q: In a fixed-pitch propeller airplane, the first indication of carburetor ice is usually
cards.why: With a fixed-pitch prop, RPM drops. With a constant-speed prop, manifold pressure drops.

cards.q: When you apply carburetor heat, the fuel/air mixture becomes
c: richer, because warm air is less dense
cards.why: Warm air is less dense, so the same fuel meets less air. RPM drops slightly at first; if there was ice, it then rises as the ice melts.

cards.q: Carburetor ice is most likely when the outside air temperature is
c: between about 20°F and 70°F with high humidity
cards.why: Fuel evaporation and the venturi can cool the air by 60°F or more, so carb ice forms even on warm, humid days, especially at low power.

cards.q: Compared with carburetors, fuel injection systems are
c: much less susceptible to induction icing
cards.why: No venturi or carburetor means no carburetor ice, though impact ice on the air filter is still possible.

cards.q: As you climb, the fuel/air mixture tends to become
c: richer, because the air is less dense
cards.why: The carburetor meters fuel by volume of air, but the air gets thinner. Lean the mixture as you climb (per the POH).

cards.q: Detonation is
c: the sudden, explosive combustion of the fuel/air mixture in the cylinder
the fuel igniting before the spark plug fires
a normal part of engine operation
cards.why: Detonation can damage the engine quickly. Causes include low-grade fuel, a too-lean mixture, high power at high temperatures and a too-steep climb.

cards.q: If you suspect detonation during a climb, you should
c: lower the nose to increase airspeed and cooling, and enrich the mixture
lean the mixture and climb more steeply
cards.why: Reduce cylinder temperatures: more cooling airflow, a richer mixture and, if needed, less power.

cards.q: Preignition is
c: the fuel/air mixture igniting before the normal spark, often from a hot spot in the cylinder
a sudden explosion after the spark
the engine running after the ignition is off because of a fuel leak
cards.why: Hot carbon deposits or a cracked spark plug can ignite the charge early, reducing power and causing roughness.

cards.q: If the grade of fuel specified for an engine isn't available, it's acceptable to use
cards.why: A lower grade can cause detonation. Use only a higher grade, or an approved STC fuel.

cards.q: Why should you drain fuel from the sumps before flight?
c: To check for water and contaminants, which settle at the low points
To make sure the tanks are not overfilled
cards.why: Water is heavier than fuel and sinks to the sumps.

cards.q: Fuel tanks should be filled after the last flight of the day mainly to
c: prevent moisture from condensing in the tanks
reduce the chance of vapor lock
keep the airplane's CG within limits
cards.why: Full tanks leave less air space for water vapor to condense overnight.

cards.q: Dual magnetos in an aircraft engine provide
c: improved engine performance and a backup ignition system
a way to start the engine without the battery
cards.why: Two magnetos and two spark plugs per cylinder burn the mixture more completely and give redundancy.

cards.q: If a magneto's ground wire is broken, the engine
c: could start if the propeller is turned by hand, even with the ignition switch off
will run on only one magneto
cards.why: A broken P-lead leaves the magneto "hot". Always treat a propeller as if the ignition is on.

cards.q: Engine oil does all of these except
cards.why: Oil lubricates, cools, seals and cleans. Air-cooled engines rely on it heavily for cooling.

cards.q: Excessively high engine temperatures can cause
c: loss of power, excessive oil consumption and possible permanent engine damage
cards.why: Common causes: low oil, too lean a mixture, a long climb at low airspeed, or operating with high power.

cards.q: On an ammeter, a positive (right) needle deflection after engine start usually means
c: the alternator is charging the battery
cards.why: Right after start the battery recharges, so the ammeter shows a charge that then decreases.

cards.q: If the ammeter shows a steady discharge in flight, you should
c: reduce electrical load and plan to land, because the alternator may have failed
ignore it if the engine is running normally
turn on more electrical equipment to test it
cards.why: The battery is running everything. Shed load (lights, unneeded radios) and land as soon as practical.

cards.q: If the alternator fails, the engine will
c: keep running, because the magnetos don't need the electrical system
cards.why: Magnetos generate their own spark. Electrically driven things (radios, flaps, lights, fuel gauges) will eventually stop.

cards.q: A circuit breaker that pops in flight
c: may be reset once, after a short cooling period, if the system is needed
should be held in to keep the system working
should be reset as many times as needed
cards.why: Popped breakers protect against overloads and fires. Reset once, after cooling; if it pops again, leave it out.

cards.q: A fixed-pitch propeller is most efficient
c: at one combination of airspeed and RPM
cards.why: Climb props are best for climbs, cruise props for cruise. Constant-speed props stay efficient over a range of speeds.

cards.q: In an airplane with a constant-speed propeller, engine power is shown by the
cards.why: The throttle controls manifold pressure and the propeller control sets RPM.

cards.q: To avoid overstressing the cylinders in a constant-speed propeller airplane, avoid
c: high manifold pressure with low RPM
low manifold pressure with high RPM
cards.why: When increasing power, increase RPM first, then manifold pressure. When reducing power, reduce manifold pressure first, then RPM.

cards.q: An abnormally high oil temperature combined with low oil pressure may mean
c: a low oil supply or a failing oil system
cards.why: Low pressure and high temperature together suggest oil loss. Plan to land soon.

cards.q: The purpose of the fuel tank vents is to
c: let air replace fuel as it's used, so fuel keeps flowing
cards.why: A blocked vent can create a vacuum in the tank and starve the engine.

cards.q: Vapor lock is most likely
c: on hot days, when fuel vaporizes in the fuel lines and blocks the flow
in cold weather with a lean mixture
when using a higher grade of fuel
cards.why: Vapor bubbles in the lines interrupt fuel flow. Fuel pumps and electric boost pumps help prevent it.

cards.q: What is the purpose of the primer?
c: To spray fuel into the intake for engine starting
To lubricate the engine before start
cards.why: The primer delivers fuel directly to the cylinders' intake ports to help a cold start.

cards.q: A rotating beacon that alternates white and green identifies
cards.why: White-green: civil land airport. White-yellow: water airport. Two quick white flashes then green: military. Green-yellow-white: heliport.

cards.q: A military airport's beacon shows
c: two quick white flashes alternating with a green flash
cards.why: Military airfields use dual-peaked white flashes between green flashes.

cards.q: The rotating beacon at an airport in Class B, C, D or E surface airspace operating during daylight hours often means
c: the ceiling is below 1,000 ft or the visibility is below 3 miles
cards.why: A daytime beacon often signals that the weather is below basic VFR minimums. Don't rely on it; there's no requirement to turn it on.

cards.q: Runway edge lights are
c: white, with yellow replacing white on the last 2,000 ft of instrument runways
cards.why: White edge lights; the caution zone (last 2,000 ft or half the runway) shows yellow on instrument runways.

cards.q: Taxiway edge lights are
cards.why: Taxiway edge lights are blue; taxiway centerline lights are green.

cards.q: From the approach end of a runway, threshold lights appear
cards.why: Threshold lights show green toward approaching aircraft and red toward aircraft at the departure end.

cards.q: Arrows on a runway leading to a white threshold bar mark
c: a displaced threshold: usable for takeoff and landing rollout, but not for landing touchdown
a blast pad that may not be used at all
cards.why: Before a displaced threshold you may taxi, take off and roll out after landing, but not touch down.

cards.q: Yellow chevrons before a runway's threshold mark
c: a blast pad or stopway, not usable for taxi, takeoff or landing
a displaced threshold usable for takeoff
cards.why: Chevron areas aren't for normal operations: they can't support aircraft.

cards.q: A large yellow or white X on a runway means
c: the runway is for emergency use only
cards.why: X marks closed runways and taxiways.

cards.q: The runway holding position markings (two solid and two dashed yellow lines across a taxiway) mean
c: stop on the solid side unless cleared onto or across the runway
yield to aircraft on the taxiway
cards.why: From the solid side you need a clearance to cross at a towered airport. From the dashed side you may cross without stopping when exiting the runway.

cards.q: When exiting a runway after landing, you are clear of the runway when
c: the whole airplane is past the holding position markings
the nose is past the runway edge line
you have turned onto the taxiway
cards.why: Taxi until all parts of the airplane are beyond the hold line, then stop unless told otherwise.

cards.q: A red sign with white letters reading "15-33" is
c: a mandatory runway holding position sign
cards.why: Red with white text: mandatory instruction. Never cross it without a clearance at a towered airport.

cards.q: A black sign with a yellow "B" and a yellow border tells you
c: taxiway B is ahead and to the right
cards.why: Black with yellow text: location sign. Yellow with black text and arrows: direction signs.

cards.q: The tetrahedron wind indicator points
c: into the wind (the small end points into the wind)
cards.why: Like a weather vane, its small end points into the wind, the direction to land. A wind sock's large open end also faces into the wind.

cards.q: Unless otherwise published, the recommended traffic pattern altitude for light airplanes is
cards.why: Recommended pattern altitude is 1,000 ft AGL for propeller airplanes, unless the Chart Supplement says otherwise.

cards.q: The recommended entry to the traffic pattern at a non-towered airport is
c: 45° to the downwind leg, abeam the midpoint of the runway, at pattern altitude
crossing over the runway at pattern altitude
cards.why: Enter at a 45° angle to downwind, abeam midfield, at pattern altitude.

cards.q: When should you make your first call on the CTAF when approaching a non-towered airport?
cards.why: Self-announce about 10 miles out, then on downwind, base, final and when leaving the runway.

cards.q: At an airport without a tower, FSS or UNICOM, you should self-announce on
cards.why: With no other facility, use MULTICOM on 122.9.

cards.q: The Automatic Terminal Information Service (ATIS) provides
c: recorded non-control information such as weather, active runway and NOTAMs
a list of traffic in the pattern
cards.why: Tell the controller you have the information by its phonetic letter, such as "with Bravo".

cards.q: How should the altitude 4,500 ft be spoken on the radio?
cards.why: Altitudes below 18,000 ft are spoken in thousands and hundreds. Numbers are said digit by digit, as with "one two zero point five".

cards.q: How is a frequency of 121.75 spoken?
c: "One two one decimal seven five zero"
cards.why: Each digit is spoken separately, with "point" for the decimal.

cards.q: The phonetic alphabet word for the letter "Q" is
cards.why: Alfa, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, Echo, Foxtrot, Golf, Hotel, India, Juliett, Kilo, Lima, Mike, November, Oscar, Papa, Quebec, Romeo, Sierra, Tango, Uniform, Victor, Whiskey, X-ray, Yankee, Zulu.

cards.q: A tower controller says "Cessna 23H, cleared for the option." You may
c: make a touch-and-go, low approach, missed approach, stop-and-go or full-stop landing
only land to a full stop
cards.why: The option lets you choose any of these. Tell the tower your intentions if asked.

cards.q: "Line up and wait" means
c: taxi onto the runway and wait for takeoff clearance
cards.why: It is not a takeoff clearance. Stay alert for traffic and ask if you've waited too long.

cards.q: If you're told to "hold short" of a runway, you must
c: stop before the holding position markings and read back the instruction
cards.why: Hold short instructions must be read back.

cards.q: Land and hold short operations (LAHSO) may be accepted by a student pilot
c: never; student pilots should not participate in LAHSO
cards.why: The AIM says student pilots shouldn't participate in LAHSO. Any pilot may decline a LAHSO clearance.

cards.q: A pilot may decline a land and hold short (LAHSO) clearance
c: at any time, for any reason, before accepting it
only if the runway is wet
cards.why: The PIC has final authority. Decline if you aren't sure you can stop in the available distance.

cards.q: When must you contact Clearance Delivery or Ground Control before taxiing at a towered airport?
c: Before moving onto the movement area (taxiways and runways)
cards.why: Ground Control controls the movement area. Ramps and aprons are non-movement areas.

cards.q: Which is the right way to scan for other aircraft during the day?
c: A series of short, regularly spaced eye movements, each covering about 10°, for about 1 second each
A continuous sweep from left to right
Staring straight ahead and relying on peripheral vision
cards.why: The eyes need to stop to detect objects. Scan sector by sector.

cards.q: An aircraft that appears to have no relative motion and keeps growing larger is
cards.why: No apparent movement means a constant bearing: you will collide unless someone changes course. It may also seem to grow slowly, then rapidly.

cards.q: Prior to starting each maneuver, such as a stall or steep turn, a pilot should
c: make clearing turns to check for traffic
cards.why: Clearing turns (usually two 90° turns) let you see the area around you before a maneuver.

cards.q: Most midair collisions occur
c: in good weather, during the day, near airports
at high altitude over the ocean
cards.why: Most happen in VFR weather near airports, often in the pattern, when pilots aren't looking out enough.

cards.q: The transponder code 1200 is used for
c: VFR flight when no other code has been assigned
cards.why: 1200 VFR. 7500 hijack, 7600 lost communications, 7700 emergency.

cards.q: If you have an emergency, you should set the transponder to
cards.why: 7700 alerts every radar facility in range. Avoid passing through 7500, 7600 or 7700 when changing codes in normal operations.

cards.q: The emergency frequency monitored by most ATC facilities and many airliners is
cards.why: 121.5 is the VHF guard frequency. ELTs also transmit on 121.5 (and 406 MHz).

cards.q: Where do you find NOTAMs for an airport you plan to use?
c: From Flight Service or an online briefing source such as the FAA NOTAM search
cards.why: NOTAMs cover runway closures, TFRs, lighting outages and more. Check them as part of every preflight.

cards.q: VASI lights showing red over red mean you are
cards.why: Red over white: all right. White over white: high. Red over red: low.

cards.q: On a four-light PAPI, two white and two red lights mean you are
cards.why: Two white, two red: on path. More white: high. More red: low. Four red: well below.

cards.q: Which airport light colors are correct for taxiway centerline lights?
cards.why: Taxiway centerline lights are green; edge lights are blue. Runway guard lights (wig-wags) are flashing yellow.

cards.q: When taxiing in a strong quartering headwind from the left, hold the ailerons
c: left aileron up (yoke turned left, into the wind)
cards.why: "Climb into a headwind, dive away from a tailwind." Headwind: aileron up on the wind side, elevator neutral. Tailwind: aileron down on the wind side, elevator down.

cards.q: Hypoxia is
c: a state of oxygen deficiency in the body sufficient to impair brain and other organ function
an excess of carbon dioxide in the blood
cards.why: Symptoms creep in unnoticed: euphoria, headache, poor judgment, blue fingernails, tunnel vision. Use oxygen and descend.

cards.q: Hypoxic hypoxia is caused by
c: the low partial pressure of oxygen at altitude
cards.why: Hypoxic: not enough oxygen available (altitude). Hypemic: blood can't carry it (CO, anemia). Stagnant: poor circulation (G-forces, cold). Histotoxic: cells can't use it (alcohol, drugs).

cards.q: Carbon monoxide poisoning causes which type of hypoxia?
cards.why: CO binds to hemoglobin far more readily than oxygen, so the blood can't carry enough oxygen.

cards.q: Alcohol and some drugs that interfere with the body's use of oxygen cause
cards.why: Histotoxic hypoxia: the cells can't use the oxygen delivered to them.

cards.q: Large accumulations of carbon monoxide in the body result in
cards.why: Symptoms include headache, drowsiness, dizziness and loss of muscle power. Turn off the heater, open the vents and land.

cards.q: Hyperventilation is
c: an abnormal increase in breathing that removes too much carbon dioxide
a lack of oxygen at altitude
the result of breathing too slowly
cards.why: Often caused by stress or anxiety. Symptoms: lightheadedness, tingling, muscle spasms. Slow your breathing, talk aloud or breathe into a bag.

cards.q: Which action helps a pilot recover from hyperventilation?
c: Slowing the breathing rate, or breathing into a paper bag or talking aloud
cards.why: Restoring the carbon dioxide level stops the symptoms.

cards.q: After a prolonged coordinated turn, an abrupt correction to level flight may create the illusion of
c: banking in the opposite direction (the leans)
cards.why: The inner ear stops sensing a long, steady turn; rolling level then feels like a bank the other way.

cards.q: The graveyard spiral illusion happens when
c: in a prolonged descending turn, the pilot senses wings level and pulls back, tightening the spiral
the pilot sees a false horizon from sloping clouds
the pilot flies over featureless terrain
cards.why: Pulling back without leveling the wings increases the turn rate and descent.

cards.q: Abrupt head movement during a prolonged constant-rate turn in IMC can cause
c: the Coriolis illusion, a strong sense of tumbling
cards.why: The Coriolis illusion is the most overwhelming of the vestibular illusions. Avoid head movements in turns.

cards.q: A runway that is narrower than usual can make you fly a final approach that is
c: lower than normal, because you think you're too high
cards.why: A narrow runway looks like a higher approach; you may descend too low. A wide runway has the opposite effect.

cards.q: An upsloping runway can create the illusion that you are
c: higher than you actually are, leading to a lower approach
cards.why: Upslope: illusion of being high, so pilots fly low. Downslope: illusion of being low, so pilots fly high.

cards.q: Rain on the windscreen can create the illusion of being
c: at a higher altitude, which can lead to a low approach
cards.why: Rain distorts the view and makes the runway look as if you're higher than you are.

cards.q: Haze can create the illusion of being
c: farther from the runway than you actually are
cards.why: Objects look farther away in haze, and you may fly a low approach.

cards.q: Flying a night approach over water or featureless terrain toward a lighted runway (a black-hole approach) can lead you to fly
cards.why: Without ground references you may feel too high and descend too low. Use the VASI/PAPI and the altimeter.

cards.q: At night, the most effective way to see a dim object is to look
c: at the object through a scanning motion only
cards.why: The rods, which work best in dim light, are around the edge of the retina, not in the center.

cards.q: At night you see a steady red light and a flashing red light ahead at your altitude. The other aircraft is
c: crossing from your right to your left
crossing from your left to your right
cards.why: The red position light is on the left wingtip. Seeing only red means you're looking at its left side, so it moves to your left.

cards.q: At night you see a steady white light and a flashing red light ahead at your altitude. The other aircraft is
cards.why: The white position light is on the tail. You're behind it.

cards.q: At night you see steady red and green lights ahead at your altitude. The other aircraft is
cards.why: Red is on the left wing, green on the right. Seeing both means it's heading toward you. Turn right.

cards.q: Small amounts of alcohol, at altitude, cause
c: greater impairment than at sea level
less impairment than at sea level
the same impairment as at sea level
cards.why: Alcohol impairs judgment and makes the body more vulnerable to hypoxia. There is no safe amount when flying.

cards.q: Before flying while taking any medication, you should
c: check with an aviation medical examiner, since many over-the-counter drugs can impair you
assume any over-the-counter drug is safe
double the time since the last dose
cards.why: 14 CFR 91.17 prohibits flying under the influence of any drug that affects your faculties. Antihistamines and sleep aids are common culprits.

cards.q: What should you do if you feel ear pain during a descent from a cold?
c: Swallow, yawn or use the Valsalva maneuver, and avoid flying with a cold
Climb immediately and stay at altitude
Descend faster to equalize the pressure
cards.why: A blocked Eustachian tube can't equalize pressure. Ear block can rupture the eardrum.

cards.q: The IMSAFE checklist is used to assess
cards.why: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion (or Eating).

cards.q: The DECIDE model of decision making begins with
c: Detect that a change has occurred
Decide on a course of action
cards.why: Detect, Estimate, Choose, Identify, Do, Evaluate.

cards.q: The 3P model of risk management is
cards.why: Perceive hazards, Process their risk, Perform risk management. Repeat it throughout the flight.

cards.q: Which hazardous attitude is described by "Don't tell me"?
cards.why: Antidote: "Follow the rules. They are usually right."

cards.q: Which hazardous attitude is described by "Do it quickly"?
cards.why: Antidote: "Not so fast. Think first."
