cards.q: Which hazardous attitude is described by "It won't happen to me"?
cards.why: Antidote: "It could happen to me."

cards.q: Which hazardous attitude is described by "I can do it"?
cards.why: Antidote: "Taking chances is foolish."

cards.q: Which hazardous attitude is described by "What's the use?"
cards.why: Antidote: "I'm not helpless. I can make a difference."

cards.q: The antidote for an impulsive attitude is
cards.why: Match each hazardous attitude with its antidote.

cards.q: "Get-there-itis" (plan continuation bias) is dangerous because it
c: makes pilots continue toward a destination despite deteriorating conditions
makes pilots turn back too early
cards.why: Set personal minimums before the flight and have a plan B.

cards.q: Scud running is
c: pushing VFR flight into lowering ceilings and visibility to keep visual contact with the ground
flying in the traffic pattern at night
cards.why: It often ends with flight into terrain or into IMC. One of the classic ADM pitfalls.

cards.q: Single-pilot resource management (SRM) is about
c: using all available resources, including ATC, passengers and automation, to manage the flight
cards.why: SRM covers task management, automation, risk management, situational awareness and CFIT awareness.

cards.q: A risk assessment matrix rates risk by combining
c: the likelihood of an event and the severity of its outcome
the weather and the time of day
cards.why: High likelihood and catastrophic severity is the highest risk. Mitigate or don't go.

cards.q: Setting personal minimums is useful because they
c: give a pre-made, objective go/no-go standard above the legal minimums
cards.why: Decide on your ceiling, visibility and wind limits on the ground, when you aren't under pressure.

cards.q: If the engine fails shortly after takeoff, the generally recommended action is to
c: lower the nose to keep airspeed and land more or less straight ahead
turn back to the runway immediately
pull the nose up to stretch the glide
cards.why: Turning back at low altitude often leads to a stall-spin. Pick a spot within about 30° of straight ahead.

cards.q: When the engine fails in cruise, what should you do first?
cards.why: Aviate first: ABC is Airspeed (best glide), Best field, Checklist. Then communicate.

cards.q: In an emergency landing in rough terrain, it's generally better to touch down
c: at the slowest possible speed under control, wings level
cards.why: Kinetic energy grows with the square of speed. Touch down as slowly as you can while still in control.

cards.q: Which statement is true about an off-airport forced landing?
c: The airframe absorbs energy, so keeping the cabin intact matters more than saving the airplane
Landing gear should always be retracted on a smooth field
It's best to land with a tailwind to keep groundspeed high
cards.why: Land into the wind, as slowly as possible, and let the wings and gear absorb energy.

cards.q: If an engine fire starts in flight, the usual first step (check the POH) is to
c: shut off the fuel supply: mixture idle cutoff and fuel selector off
climb to put out the fire
cards.why: Starve the fire of fuel, then land as soon as possible. A steep descent at higher speed may help extinguish it.

cards.q: If you smell burning insulation (an electrical fire), the usual first action is to
cards.why: Then turn off all other switches (except ignition), close vents, and land as soon as possible.

cards.q: If you inadvertently fly into IMC as a VFR pilot, the generally recommended action is to
c: keep the wings level on the instruments and make a gentle 180° turn back to VFR
descend quickly to get below the clouds
climb steeply to get on top
cards.why: Trust the attitude indicator, make a standard-rate (or shallower) turn and ask ATC for help.

cards.q: The ELT in most US aircraft transmits on
cards.why: Satellites monitor only 406 MHz signals. 121.5 is used for homing.

cards.q: When flying at night, a pilot should use
c: the position lights, anticollision lights and, near airports, the landing light
no lights to preserve night vision
cards.why: Position lights are required from sunset to sunrise. Landing lights make you more visible.

cards.q: Slow flight is practised to help you
c: recognize the airplane's handling near the stall and maintain control at high angles of attack
fly the fastest possible traffic pattern
cards.why: Near the stall the controls feel mushy and more power and rudder are needed. ACS: altitude ±100 ft, airspeed +10/−0 kt, no stall warning.

cards.q: The first step in recovering from any stall is to
cards.why: Pitch nose down to reduce the angle of attack, level the wings, then add power as needed. Add right rudder for the power.

cards.q: A go-around should begin with
c: applying takeoff power and adjusting pitch to stop the descent
retracting all the flaps at once
cards.why: Power first, pitch to climb attitude, then clean up flaps in stages. Retracting all flaps at once can make the airplane sink.

cards.q: During a forward slip, the airplane's
c: longitudinal axis points at an angle to its flight path, increasing drag and descent rate
nose stays aligned with the flight path
cards.why: A forward slip uses opposite aileron and rudder to lose altitude without gaining airspeed. A sideslip corrects for crosswind on landing.

cards.q: In a crosswind landing using the wing-low method, you lower the
c: upwind wing and use opposite rudder to keep the nose aligned with the runway
downwind wing with rudder toward the wind
upwind wing and rudder toward the wind
cards.why: Aileron into the wind stops the drift; opposite rudder aligns the nose. Touch down on the upwind main wheel first.

cards.q: On a soft-field takeoff, you should
c: keep weight off the nosewheel, lift off as soon as possible and accelerate in ground effect
hold the airplane on the ground until well above Vy
use full flaps for every soft-field takeoff
cards.why: Get the nosewheel off the soft surface early, lift off at a low speed, then accelerate to Vx or Vy in ground effect.

cards.q: On a short-field takeoff over an obstacle, you should climb at
c: Vx until clear of the obstacle, then Vy
cards.why: Vx gives the most altitude per distance. Once clear, transition to Vy.

cards.q: The ACS standard for altitude during steep turns for a private pilot is
cards.why: Steep turns: 45° bank ±5°, altitude ±100 ft, airspeed ±10 kt, roll out on heading ±10°.

cards.q: When practicing ground reference maneuvers such as turns around a point, the steepest bank occurs when
c: the airplane is headed directly downwind
the airplane is headed directly upwind
cards.why: Groundspeed is highest downwind, so the bank must be steepest there to keep a constant radius.

cards.q: Wingtip vortices tend to
c: sink and spread out behind the airplane
stay at the generating aircraft's altitude
cards.why: They sink about 300 to 500 fpm and level off 500 to 1,000 ft below the flight path.

cards.q: Near the ground, wake vortices drift outward at about
c: they don't move once on the ground
cards.why: Within 100 to 200 ft of the ground they move laterally at 2 to 3 knots. A light crosswind can stall one vortex over the runway.

cards.q: Which wind condition is most likely to keep a wake vortex over the landing runway?
cards.why: A light quartering tailwind can move the vortices into the touchdown zone of the following aircraft.

cards.q: Departing behind a large jet that just took off, you should
c: lift off before the jet's rotation point and climb above its flight path
lift off after its rotation point
cards.why: Its vortices start at rotation, so be airborne before that point and stay above its path, or wait.

cards.q: Taking off behind a large jet that just landed, you should lift off
c: beyond the point where the jet touched down
before the point where the jet touched down
at any point, since vortices stop at touchdown
cards.why: The landing jet's vortices exist up to its touchdown point. Lift off past it.

cards.q: Which aircraft generates the strongest wake turbulence?
c: A heavy airplane, in a clean configuration, flying slowly
A light airplane at high speed
A heavy airplane with full flaps at high speed
cards.why: Weight, slow speed and a clean wing produce the strongest vortices.

cards.q: Hovering and slow-moving helicopters produce
c: a strong downwash and vortices that can be as dangerous as an airplane's
cards.why: Avoid taxiing or flying within three rotor diameters of a hovering helicopter.

cards.q: Wake turbulence separation for a light aircraft departing behind a heavy jet from the same runway is normally
c: 2 minutes (or 3 minutes from an intersection), applied by ATC
cards.why: ATC applies time-based wake separation, but you can request more. The pilot still owns wake avoidance.

cards.q: When ATC issues "caution wake turbulence", the responsibility for avoiding the wake is
c: shared equally with the other pilot
cards.why: Pilots are expected to adjust their flight path to avoid wake encounters.

cards.q: Crossing behind a large jet en route, you should
c: fly above its flight path or wait, rather than crossing below and behind it
cross immediately behind it at the same altitude
cards.why: Vortices sink, so cross above. Avoid the area below and behind a large aircraft.

cards.q: Jet blast from a taxiing jet can be hazardous
c: for hundreds of feet behind the jet, even at idle power
cards.why: Stay well clear behind jets on the ground and position yourself to avoid their exhaust.

cards.q: The greatest risk of a wake encounter on approach is when you are
c: below and behind the generating aircraft
above and behind the generating aircraft
abeam the generating aircraft at a higher altitude
cards.why: Because vortices sink, stay at or above the larger aircraft's path.

cards.q: A wake vortex encounter can cause
c: a sudden, uncommanded roll that may exceed the airplane's roll control
only a slight bump with no control problems
cards.why: The induced roll can exceed what the ailerons can counter, especially for small aircraft.
